43bd301fdba2f9ec: KUCHING, Oct 28 — The Sessions Court here has sentenced a soldier with the rank of lance corporal to a total of 34 years’ jail and 14 strokes of the rotan for two counts of raping his wife’s niece, who was then 12 years old, in 2023.
Judge Iris Awen Jon convicted the 29-year-old following a full trial with both charges framed under Section 376(1) of the Penal Code.
For the first charge, he was sentenced to 16 years behind bars and six strokes of the rotan, while for the second charge, he received 18 years’ imprisonment and eight strokes.
Iris ordered both sentences to run concurrently from the date of his remand on September 20, 2024, effectively amounting to 18 years’ imprisonment.
She also ordered the accused to undergo rehabilitative counselling throughout his detention, in accordance with Section 26 of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act (SOACA) 2017.
Iris further ordered the accused to be placed under police supervision for two years upon completing his custodial sentence, pursuant to Section 27(1) of SOACA 2017.
According to the charges, the man raped the victim, who was 12 years old at the time, in two separate incidents on December 20, 2023 and January 2024, at an Armed Forces Family Quarters here.
The first incident occurred while the victim was sleeping at the man’s house, when he pushed her onto a mattress and raped her while covering her mouth as she attempted to resist.
In the second incident, the man pulled the victim’s shirt, causing her to fall, before removing her trousers and raping her.
Following the incidents, the victim lodged a police report, which led to his arrest.
In her judgment, Iris found that the prosecution had successfully proven its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt after assessing all the evidence presented throughout the trial.

She also found that the defence witnesses’ testimony carried less evidential weight, adding that no independent evidence was presented to show that the man was not in Sarawak at the time of the incidents, despite the defence having produced flight tickets.

Throughout the full trial, the prosecution, represented by deputy public prosecutors Mohamad Aiman Mutallib Mohamad Shariff and Chuah Kai Sheng, called six witnesses, while the defence presented three witnesses.
The accused was represented by counsel Joshua Lee Sik Ern. — The Borneo Post

8663b45578dae0d7: KUALA LUMPUR: Moto3 rookie Hakim Danish Ramli will be determined to rediscover his early-season form when he takes to the track for the Petronas Grand Prix of Malaysia which starts on Friday.
The Aeon Credit-MT Helmets-MSI rider had a strong first half of the season, finishing third at Mugello and winning his maiden GP at Brno, both in June.
But his form has tapered since the summer break. He has only finished in the top-10 once, a ninth-place finish at the Red Bull Ring last month, since winning the Czech GP.
His poor run of form continued at Phillip Island last week, where he qualified 23rd. The race was, however, cancelled due to poor visibility.
Danish made it clear that he is determined not to let his supporters down at his home GP.
"This is my home race week, and I am very happy and excited to compete at the Malaysian GP," said Danish today.
"I am certainly feeling even more motivated to race and cannot wait to get out on track this weekend.
"Of course, I want to give my very best for the team, Malaysia, my family and everyone who has supported me.
"I hope to perform at my best throughout the weekend."
The 19-year-old's familiarity with Sepang Circuit - the track he essentially grew up riding - should give him added confidence heading into the weekend.
Danish has already experienced racing the Malaysian GP as he was given a Moto3 wildcard last season.
The Terengganu-born rider impressed on his debut. He made it into the faster qualifying two (Q2) group last year and was fighting for a top-10 position during the race.
The race, however, ended on a disappointing note as Danish was forced to retire from the race due to a technical issue with his bike just five laps from the finish.
Danish is currently ninth overall in the lightweight class standings on 103 points.

CFMoto Gaviota Aspar Team's Maximo Quiles leads the championship on 351 points. Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP's David Almansa (217 points) and Red Bull KTM Ajo's Brian Uriarte (198 points) are second and third overall.
02454053b37ace99: JOHOR BARU: Five people, including two federal enforcement officers, have been arrested for allegedly soliciting and receiving about RM1 million in bribes to shield foreign workers from enforcement action.

The five suspects, comprising three men and two women aged between their 40s and 60s, were arrested between 10am and 4pm yesterday in an operation conducted in Selangor and Johor.
6ad3d7ab7b5c8a2e: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian educators are more confident than their global peers that their institutions are keeping pace with artificial intelligence (AI) developments, according to a study by Pearson and Amazon Web Services (AWS).
The study found that 49 per cent of Malaysian educators believe their institutions are keeping pace with most or all AI developments, compared with the cross-market average of 32 per cent.
The report, titled AI Readiness: Building the Bridge from Higher Education to Work, found that educators were considerably more confident than learners and employers.
This suggests that institutional assessments might not fully reflect students' experiences or workplace expectations.
The study also found that Malaysians perceive AI-driven change to be happening rapidly.
Some 71 per cent of learners and 70 per cent of educators described the pace of change as extremely or very fast, exceeding the cross-market average of 67 per cent.
Among employers, 61 per cent shared that view, broadly in line with the cross-market average.

Pearson vice-president of APAC Enterprise Learning and Skills Craig McFarlane said Malaysia had laid the foundations for its AI ambitions through national momentum, engaged institutions, active employers and confident learners.
"The opportunity now is to turn that momentum into consistent, workplace-relevant outcomes," he said at the report's launch here today.

To achieve this, he said, institutions would need to help educators keep pace with AI developments, incorporate practical learning, strengthen collaboration with employers and ensure responsible AI use through effective governance.
Despite differences in perceptions of AI readiness, confidence in the value of higher education remains strong.
The study found that 80 per cent of higher education leaders and 76 per cent of employers believe AI makes university education more important rather than less.
The report classified Malaysia as a "Fragmented Adaptive" market, where the main challenge is translating interest in AI readiness into consistent, well-governed and professionally relevant outcomes.

It said closer cooperation among educational institutions, employers and policymakers would be crucial to translating confidence in AI into practical capabilities and preparing graduates for the workplace.

The report also stressed the importance of timely action in achieving Malaysia's AI policy ambitions, particularly given estimates that AI could contribute up to US$115 billion to the country's gross domestic product by 2030.
The study surveyed more than 2,700 respondents across Malaysia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and Vietnam.
Malaysia accounted for 402 respondents, comprising 300 learners, 51 educators and 51 employers.

3ea148063c651c77: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — The Federal Court here today allowed Datuk Seri Najib Tun Razak’s application to attend the hearing of his application for leave to appeal in a bid to revive his RM1.9 million lawsuit against former Attorney General Tan Sri Tommy Thomas.

A three-judge panel chaired by Chief Judge of Malaya Datuk Seri Hashim Hamzah allowed the application after Najib’s counsel, S. Bala Ravi, requested an order to produce (OTP) to enable the former prime minister to attend the proceedings from prison.
The order would allow Najib to attend the leave-to-appeal hearing and, should leave be granted, the substantive appeal hearing.
Also on the panel were Federal Court judges Datuk Mohd Nazlan Mohd Ghazali and Datuk Azmi Ariffin.
The leave-to-appeal application is scheduled to be heard on November 26.

Najib, 73, filed a notice of motion on February 10 this year seeking leave to appeal against the entire Court of Appeal decision, which upheld the High Court’s order striking out his lawsuit. He has submitted three questions of law for the Federal Court’s consideration.

On January 13 this year, a three-judge Court of Appeal panel upheld the High Court’s decision to strike out the suit, ruling that the action was premature because the relevant criminal proceedings had not commenced when the lawsuit was filed.
On November 25, 2022, the High Court allowed Thomas’s application to strike out the suit without a full trial.

Najib, the former Pekan Member of Parliament, filed the lawsuit on October 22, 2021, alleging that Thomas had abused his power in bringing charges against him in connection with the 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) case.
In the suit, Najib alleged that Thomas had acted with malicious intent in prosecuting him in cases involving 1MDB and International Petroleum Investment Company (IPIC).

The charges included abuse of power under Section 23 of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2009 and several counts of money laundering under the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001.

Najib is seeking, among other relief, a declaration that Thomas committed misfeasance in public office. He is also claiming RM1.9 million in special damages for expenses incurred in appointing an audit team to review documents and prepare his defence in the criminal proceedings.
Thomas served as Attorney General from June 4, 2018, to February 28, 2020. — Bernama
00f63b57f3e55de3: JAKARTA: Hundreds of Indonesian security personnel were deployed on Wednesday in anticipation of student protests against several of President Prabowo Subianto's policies, as well as his government's handling of forest fires.
Students from the University of Indonesia said they were set to stage protests in several spots in the capital Jakarta.

They are calling on the government to declare the ongoing wildfires in Sumatra and Borneo a national disaster, and to halt spending on populist programmes such as Prabowo's free meals scheme, among other demands.
Wednesday's protests carry the hashtag #IndonesiaAware, the students said.
It is unclear how many students will take to the streets.
A heavy police and military presence, as well as armoured vehicles, could be seen in busy parts of central Jakarta on Wednesday morning.
Protests have also been held in haze-stricken areas of Borneo and Sumatra, including one in Central Kalimantan last week.
Prabowo's approval ratings have fallen steadily since late last year, according to surveys by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC), two years into his presidency.
Indonesia's last major protest took place in August, when hundreds were detained, and students also held demonstrations last week.
In 2025, weeks-long nationwide protests broke out in Indonesia after the police killing of a motorcycle taxi driver, with several more people killed during the unrest. -REUTERS

5f04cb8983f77d92: KUALA LUMPUR: Nearly seven in 10 Malaysian employers say difficulty finding graduates with the right skills is a major challenge as artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more widely adopted in the workplace, a study found.
The study by Pearson and Amazon Web Services (AWS) highlights a gap between higher education and workplace expectations as Malaysia pursues its ambition to become an AI Nation by 2030.
It found that 69 per cent of Malaysian employers face this challenge, while 45 per cent cited graduates' lack of practical experience or ability to apply their skills.

The findings highlight a disconnect between graduates' confidence in their job readiness and employers' expectations of the practical skills, professional maturity and human judgment needed to work effectively alongside AI.
While 77 per cent of Malaysian learners believe they are ready to enter the workforce, only 70 per cent say their university education is preparing them well for the workplace.
The report, titled "AI Readiness: Building the Bridge from Higher Education to Work", also found differences in the skills educators and employers consider important.
Educators place greater emphasis on the ability to use AI tools, while employers prioritise communication, collaboration and the ability to combine human judgment with AI capabilities.
The study found that 47 per cent of Malaysian educators prioritise the ability to use AI tools, while 45 per cent emphasise creativity and innovation.
In contrast, 51 per cent of employers prioritise communication and collaboration, while an equal proportion value graduates' ability to combine human judgment with AI capabilities.
Another 41 per cent of employers consider adaptability an important skill for graduates entering an AI-driven workplace.
AWS general manager of global education Valerie Singer said employers wanted graduates who could apply AI to solve real-world problems rather than merely understand or use the technology.

"We see that employers want graduates who can apply AI to solve real problems and are working to make sure what students learn actually prepares them for the workforce," she said at the report's launch here today.
Singer said stronger dialogue between employers and educators could help address concerns over graduates' lack of practical experience, professional maturity and human judgment.
The findings suggest that closer collaboration between higher education institutions and industry is needed to equip graduates with the skills employers require.
Nearly half of Malaysian learners, or 49 per cent, said more practical experience would increase the value of their education, while 37 per cent wanted more opportunities to solve problems using AI.
More than half of learners (52 per cent) and employers (53 per cent) favoured a hybrid model that places equal importance on university education and practical work experience.

The report also introduced the AI Readiness Friction Framework, designed to help education and industry leaders identify and address six barriers in the transition from education to employment: pace, connection, capability, governance, experience and skills.
The framework provides recommendations to help institutions and employers overcome these barriers and improve graduates' transition into the workforce.
The study surveyed more than 2,700 students, educators and employers across six countries: Malaysia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and Vietnam.
Malaysia accounted for 402 respondents, comprising 300 learners, 51 educators and 51 employers. The survey was supplemented by in-depth interviews with higher education leaders.

d7699f0a79007166: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — DAP lawmaker RSN Rayer today called on the police to explain why the investigation into the death of Noorizwan Zulkefly was classified voluntarily hurt instead of murder.

Rayer cited news reports quoting Bukit Aman Criminal Investigation Department director Datuk M Kumar, who said the death-in-detention case is investigated under Section 331 of the Penal Code, which deals with voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort a confession or force the restoration of property.
The member of parliament for Jelutong said he felt the police decision was hasty, as the postmortem report on Noorizwan’s death had yet to be ready, with the cause of death still undetermined.
“I don’t agree that it’s being investigated under 331. By right it should be 302 of the Penal Code (murder),” Rayer said at a press conference in the Parliament building here.

“If the complete postmortem report is not even ready, why is the police seemingly hasty to classify it under Section 331? I am quoting the CID chief. But my question is if the complete report isn’t even ready, the cause of death is yet to be determined, why is the police rushing to classify it as 331?” The MP added.
Noorizwan, 42, died on October 1, while under detention at the Cheras district police headquarters lock-up.
News reports, quoting family members and their lawyers, indicated Noorizwan suffered nearly two dozen severe injuries based on preliminary postmortem findings.

Bukit Aman had classified the case under Section 331 following statements recorded by a forensic medical consultant at Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz who conducted the postmortem, Kumar was quoted as saying.
The medical consultant confirmed signs of external injuries on several parts of the deceased’s body that are consistent with blunt-force trauma and was not self-inflicted, Kumar said.
The case has since drawn national attention and revived public scrutiny on the government’s pledge to reform detention procedures and end custodial deaths.
Addressing Parliament yesterday, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail pledged transparency in investigation and to punish the officers involved.
But Rayer said the authorities have not indicated if the officers who interrogated Noorizwan had been suspended.
“In any investigation papers, the officers involved will be named explicitly. So who are the officers who took Noorizwan out from the lock-up to be investigated, who are they?” The MP asked.

“Have they been identified? Have they been suspended with immediate effect? These are the questions they must answer. It’s not enough to issue the same statements that the case is being investigated.”
8ed4f3a9fe88939a: KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) has asked online platforms to remove 65,680 instances of harmful fake content since 2023, the Dewan Rakyat was told.

Deputy Communications Minister Teo Nie Ching said 56,304, or 86 per cent, of the flagged content had been taken down following requests made between Jan 1, 2023, and Oct 15, 2026, under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and the Online Safety Act 2025.
During the same period, MCMC investigated 546 cases involving false content under Section 233 of the 1998 Act.
Nineteen cases were brought to court, of which 12 have been decided, resulting in total fines of RM75,500. Compounds totalling RM1.72 million were imposed in 34 cases.
Warning letters were issued in 74 cases, while 29 remained under investigation. Another 390 cases were classified as requiring no further action.

Teo was responding to Datuk Rosol Wahid (PN-Hulu Terengganu) during the Dewan Rakyat's oral question-and-answer session. Rosol had sought statistics on fake news cases since 2023, the action taken and penalties imposed.
Teo said the ministry would continue strengthening legal and enforcement efforts to curb fake news and keep the digital space safe, responsible and trustworthy.

In a supplementary question, Rosol asked who determined whether content was fake news – MCMC, the government or the courts – and what checks and balances prevented enforcement action from being used to silence legitimate criticism of the government.
Teo said MCMC assessed complaints from government agencies, enforcement agencies and the public, and requested takedowns from platforms if it believed the law might have been breached.
"But the platforms also make their own assessment of whether the content violates the law or their community guidelines," she said, explaining why not all requests resulted in takedowns.
She said the courts also played a role, noting that many accused had pleaded guilty.
"When someone is charged in court, they have the right to defend themselves, but at the same time we see the court's decision," she said.

Suhaizan Kaiat (PH-Pulai) said the number of prosecutions was small compared with the number of takedowns, while fake news remained widespread. He asked what further measures the ministry would take to impose harsher penalties.
Teo said MCMC decided whether to investigate cases based on advice from the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC), which determined whether to prosecute, impose a compound or take no further action.
addd5ae75a2aa218: SHANGHAI: France soccer captain Kylian Mbappe apologised to China on Tuesday after a fierce backlash over his comments referring to late Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator, underscoring how swiftly global celebrities can come unstuck.
In a video on a French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappe is heard discussing a funny meme where his face had been photoshopped on to that of "some guy — I think he's a Chinese dictator."

"During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself," Real Madrid forward Mbappe said in a statement. "My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset," added Mbappe, who has ties with firms including Swiss sportswear brand On Holding, hotel chain Accor and Lego. "This was absolutely not my intention."

The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative China market, where satire about Mao, modern China's founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.
LaLiga President Javier Tebas said that he held a meeting with the ambassador of China in Spain to address the situation and "seek solutions that allow us to overcome this episode."

"Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of Chinese fans who follow our competitions," Tebas said in a statement posted to social media. "China is and will continue to be a strategic partner for LaLiga."
Other major organisations that have incurred the wrath of Beijing and Chinese netizens include fashion brand Dolce & Gabbana, Swiss watchmaker Swatch and the National Basketball Association.
Some recovered quickly while others took years.
Brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage said they were ceasing all cooperation with Mbappe effective immediately.
The companies said they "firmly oppose and have zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people."

China's state television has halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving LaLiga and Mbappe, and all advertisements involving Mbappe have been removed, state-backed media outlet the Paper reported on Tuesday.
"Mbappe's team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about," said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T. Burns Sports Group.
Swiss-based On Holding, which signed Mbappe in September after he had spent two decades at US rival Nike, welcomed his apology and said it had "deep respect" for China.
Accor did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Denmark's Lego, which has a Mbappe building set on sale in China, said it could not comment. The Mbappe set still featured on Lego's Chinese website on Tuesday.

Chinese state media outlet China Daily said Mbappe's remark had "triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence."

"What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it," the state-backed Global Times added. "The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn't get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance."
On Chinese social media platform Weibo, one user wrote about the apology; "Not accepted. Not forgiven!!".
State broadcaster CCTV struck a more conciliatory tone, however, saying it would listen to what Mbappe had to say after his apology, and "even more importantly" watch what he does.
"We hope La Liga, Real Madrid, and Mbappe himself will genuinely learn a lesson from this, offer a sincere apology, and thoroughly correct their mistakes," CCTV said in a statement.
Real Madrid declined to comment.
Tebas issued an apology earlier on Tuesday on X and said his organisation deeply regretted the alleged comments that have caused discomfort and offence in China.

"We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation," Tebas wrote. "A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single episode."

As of 0700 GMT, four topics related to Mbappe were still among the top 10 trending searches on Weibo. Some netizens called for China to blacklist Mbappe and reduce his commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes.
Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe's face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for.
Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.

"In attempting to laugh at himself and his reputation of being a dictator in the locker room, he apparently crossed a red line he didn't know was there," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.

In an interview with L'Equipe last month, Mbappe said that although aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting him as a dictator showed "a lack of political and human awareness."

A spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry said words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people "will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."-Reuters

c8cd83f9c1e4d530: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — The Ministry of Education (MOE) plans to expand the K11 Comprehensive School Programme to 10 more schools next year to improve access to education from primary to secondary level, particularly in rural areas.

Deputy Education Minister Wong Kah Woh said nine schools had implemented the programme since its introduction in 2023, enabling students to complete their education from Year One to Form Five under one roof.
He said the pilot programme was first introduced at Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan (SMK) Long Bedian in Sarawak and SMK Benta in Pahang.

“We are aware that some schools are not yet ready to transition to K9 or K11 schools. However, provided the conditions are suitable, the ministry will ensure that access to education remains available,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat today.
He added that the ministry provided 18 types of assistance to schoolchildren in both urban and rural areas.

Wong was responding to a question from Datuk Mohd Kurniawan Naim Moktar (BN-Kinabatangan) on the ministry’s strategic action plan to address the risk of long-term school dropout among students from multidimensionally hardcore poor households.
He said the ministry continued to narrow the educational gap through targeted interventions and periodic curriculum improvements as part of its long-term strategy.
Under the District Transformation Programme, targeted interventions were implemented in 744 schools in 2025, benefiting 41,817 students across six core subjects.
The initiatives aimed to address disparities in academic achievement based on geographical location, socioeconomic background and gender.
Wong said the proportion of rural Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) candidates eligible to receive their certificates rose from 92.31 per cent in 2024 to 92.9 per cent in 2025.
Meanwhile, the gender gap in certificate eligibility rates narrowed from 5.95 percentage points to 5.32 percentage points over the same period.

He said the targeted interventions, academic support and curriculum improvements reflected the ministry’s commitment to promoting educational equity and ensuring that every student had access to quality education, regardless of socioeconomic background. — Bernama
31dedccc68e40904: KUALA LUMPUR: Jelutong member of parliament RSN Rayer wants the police and the attorney-general to investigate the death of Noorizwan Zulkefly in custody as murder, arguing that the current classification of the case is premature.

Rayer was responding to Federal Criminal Investigation Department director Datuk M. Kumar, who said the case was being investigated under Section 331 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort a confession or compel the restoration of property.
Rayer said Section 331 was not the appropriate provision
"It should be investigated under Section 302 of the Penal Code (for murder)," he told a press conference in parliament here.
He questioned how the police could classify the case before the full post-mortem report and confirmed cause of death were available.
"If the complete post-mortem report has not been obtained and the cause of death is also unknown, why are the police in such a hurry to classify this case under Section 331?" he asked.
Rayer said the attorney-general should be the one to decide on the classification of the case.
He asked whether the investigating officers directly involved had been identified and who took Noorizwan out of the lock-up to question him.
"Have they been suspended from duty immediately? These are my questions," he said.
Rayer called for the policemen involved to be suspended, especially the investigating officer and the intelligence team assigned to interrogate Noorizwan.
"The injuries suffered by the late Noorizwan clearly justify, indeed demand, an investigation under Section 302 of the Penal Code, not Section 331," he said.
Previously, Kumar said a post-mortem found external injuries on several parts of Noorizwan's body, consistent with blunt-force trauma and not self-inflicted.
He said the police had yet to obtain the full post-mortem report to confirm the cause of death.
Noorizwan, 42, died on Oct 1 after about 10 days in custody at the Cheras police headquarters.
His family's lawyer, N Surendran, has said a pathologist told the family that he died from blunt force trauma, and has also urged police to investigate the case under Section 302.
8c378368aee3fad5: SYDNEY, Oct 28 — Australian mushroom murderer Erin Patterson will learn Friday if she has succeeded in overturning her conviction for killing three people with a poisoned beef Wellington lunch.
Patterson, 52, was found guilty last year of murdering her husband’s parents and an elderly aunt in 2023 by serving them a beef-and-pastry meal laced with lethal death cap mushrooms.
A judge sentenced her to life imprisonment, eligible for parole after 33 years.
In August this year, her lawyers argued before the Court of Appeal in Melbourne that she had suffered a miscarriage of justice.
They alleged a litany of irregularities in the trial, including an “oppressive” cross-examination and unfair decisions on the admission of evidence.
Prosecutors also appealed, however, saying her 33-year non-parole period was “manifestly inadequate” — and she should never be allowed to walk free.
On Friday morning, the Court of Appeal will hand down its decision on both appeals, officials said.
On the conviction, the judges must decide whether there are even grounds to give her leave to appeal.
If they agree to do so, the judges may dismiss the appeal or uphold it, in which case they may order a new trial or acquit her.
On her sentence, the court will either dismiss the prosecution’s appeal or uphold it and re-sentence her.
Patterson was not expected to attend in person.
Her trial last year drew podcasters, film crews and true crime fans to a courthouse in the rural town of Morwell, a sedate hamlet in Victoria better known for its prize-winning roses.
Audiences from New York to New Delhi followed every twist of what many now simply call the “mushroom murders”.
The motive of the killings remains a mystery.

A 12-person jury found Patterson guilty in July last year of murdering her husband Simon’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, as well as his aunt, Heather Wilkinson, at her home in the Victorian farming village of Leongatha.
She was also found guilty of attempting to murder Heather’s husband Ian, a pastor who fell gravely ill but eventually recovered. — AFP
1eb532f150ec7ca2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Malaysia must strengthen proactive cybersecurity measures as cybercriminals increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to automate attacks, identify vulnerabilities and create more convincing scams, said Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Datuk Chang Lih Kang.

He said traditional security measures alone were no longer sufficient to address increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, requiring organisations to adopt continuous monitoring, early threat detection and proactive security measures.

“If attackers are using AI to become faster and more sophisticated, we must ensure that our defenders are equipped to stay ahead. Ultimately, our objective should be to prevent cyber incidents wherever possible, rather than simply responding after damage has occurred.

“AI itself can become a powerful tool for cybersecurity professionals, helping them identify suspicious activities, analyse vulnerabilities and respond more effectively to emerging threats,” he said when officiating the LGMS AI Cybersecurity Summit 2026 here today.

Chang said organisations must protect AI applications, models and data alongside conventional information technology infrastructure, with responsible AI adoption supported by technical safeguards, risk management and human oversight.

The minister said the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (Mosti) had developed the National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE), outlining seven principles for responsible AI development and use, including privacy, security, transparency and accountability.
Chang said cybersecurity also presented opportunities for Malaysia to develop homegrown technologies and intellectual property under the “Made by Malaysia” aspiration highlighted in Budget 2027.

“Ultimately, the ‘Made by Malaysia’ aspiration is not simply about producing technology locally. It is about creating high-value jobs, developing Malaysian intellectual property and ensuring that our country captures greater economic value from technological advancement,” he said.

In this regard, he welcomed LGMS Bhd’s unveiling of five Malaysian-developed cybersecurity solutions addressing AI application security, software vulnerabilities, credential exposure, digital attack surfaces and cyber intrusions.
The five solutions unveiled today were AI & LLM Application Security Assessment, NOVA, SPECTA, AI-driven Attack Surface Management and Next-generation Deception.

6e9575b14272cb3d: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Former Bersatu member Badrul Hisham Shaharin, better known as Chegubard, has been sentenced to four months in jail for criminal defamation over remarks tarnishing the King’s reputation.

c436d0d4cb157b6f: DAMASCUS: Syria reopened its main border crossing with Jordan on Wednesday as the two countries reaffirmed ties that were strained by a deadly retaliatory strike by Jordanian forces.
Jordan's strike – a reprisal against a gun attack on a church – sparked the worst crisis between the two countries since the ousting of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Syria condemned the strikes on the country's south as an "unacceptable violation", while Jordan said it killed more than 20 jihadist fighters in its raid.
Jordan sought to ease tensions on Tuesday, saying it had "great respect" for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.

The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of Wednesday morning, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA.

Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan's Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 – prompting a military response from Amman.
While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria's civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children.

On Tuesday, Jordan's Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan's "full respect for Syria's sovereignty... and security", while also expressing "sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims", according to a joint statement.
The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as "Daesh sites", using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group.
Earlier, Jordan's government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that "the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh's ranks – estimated at more than 20 fighters."
He also said "a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation" had been destroyed.
'Blatant violation'
Earlier, Syria's foreign ministry issued a "condemnation and rejection" of the strikes, calling them "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination."
It also said the raid was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty."
In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.
"We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children – two boys and a girl – were killed," said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag.
An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family's destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble.

Syrian Emergencies and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Tuesday that both sides were handling the dispute through "diplomatic and legal channels" with the aim of securing justice for the victims.
'Dark ideologies'
On Monday, Amman said authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage.
Authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.
"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," King Abdullah II said.
IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country's more than 13-year civil war.
But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces.
The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province.

9b69d753d7dd1034: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must strengthen proactive cybersecurity measures as cybercriminals increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to automate attacks, identify vulnerabilities and create more convincing scams.

"If attackers are using AI to become faster and more sophisticated, we must ensure that our defenders are equipped to stay ahead. Ultimately, our objective should be to prevent cyber incidents wherever possible, rather than simply responding after damage has occurred.

"AI itself can become a powerful tool for cybersecurity professionals, helping them identify suspicious activities, analyse vulnerabilities and respond more effectively to emerging threats," he said when officiating the LGMS AI Cybersecurity Summit 2026 here today.

Chang said organisations must protect AI applications, models and data alongside conventional information technology infrastructure, with responsible AI adoption supported by technical safeguards, risk management and human oversight.

He said the Science, Technology and Innovation Ministry had developed the National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE), which outline seven principles for responsible AI development and use, including privacy, security, transparency and accountability.
Chang said cybersecurity also offered opportunities for Malaysia to develop homegrown technologies and intellectual property under the "Made by Malaysia" aspiration highlighted in the 2027 Budget.

"Ultimately, the 'Made by Malaysia' aspiration is not simply about producing technology locally. It is about creating high-value jobs, developing Malaysian intellectual property and ensuring that our country captures greater economic value from technological advancement," he said.

He welcomed LGMS Bhd's unveiling of five Malaysian-developed cybersecurity solutions covering AI application security, software vulnerabilities, credential exposure, digital attack surfaces and cyber intrusions.

Chang said Malaysia must also expand its pool of cybersecurity specialists, engineers, researchers and AI professionals through closer collaboration among universities, research institutions, government agencies and industry to create high-value jobs and capture greater economic value from technological advancement.
9777f2ad7ebf598d: JERUSALEM: Israelis voted on Tuesday in their highest turnout for decades, with exit polls showing the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his rival are neck and neck.

Exit polls from the three mainstream Israeli television networks gave the two blocs around 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset – well below the 61 needed to govern – after initially giving an edge to the opposition led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. COALITION
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government – not necessarily the party with the most seats.

The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
It took Netanyahu 58 days to form his government after the previous election in November 2022.
2. MINORITY GOVERNMENT
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties – whose community makes up 20 per cent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian – could play a critical role.

Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for anyone that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said that an especially high Arab turnout "indicates a strong desire for partnership."
Eisenkot has not even entertained the possibility publicly, and Netanyahu relentlessly told Jewish voters in his campaign that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
"Bottom line, at the moment, it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results," Elovitz said.
3. NATIONAL UNITY GOVERNMENT
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, the prospect of a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.

Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on Oct 16 found that 55 per cent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.

This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.

A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
4. DEADLOCK AND NEW ELECTIONS
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.

The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.--AFP

Jordan sought to ease tensions on Tuesday, saying it had "great respect" for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.

The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of Wednesday morning, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA.

Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan's Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 – prompting a military response from Amman.
While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria's civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children.

On Tuesday, Jordan's foreign minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan's "full respect for Syria's sovereignty... and security", while also expressing "sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims", according to a joint statement.
The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as "Daesh sites", using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group.
Earlier, Jordan's government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that "the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh's ranks – estimated at more than 20 fighters".
He also said "a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation" had been destroyed.
'Blatant violation'
Earlier, Syria's foreign ministry issued a "condemnation and rejection" of the strikes, calling them "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination".
It also said the raid was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty".
In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.
"We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children – two boys and a girl – were killed," said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag.
An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family's destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble.

Syrian emergency and disaster management minister Raed al-Saleh said on Tuesday that both sides were handling the dispute through "diplomatic and legal channels" with the aim of securing justice for the victims.
'Dark ideologies'
On Monday, Amman said authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage.
Authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between 2% and 3% of the population.
"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," King Abdullah II said.
IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country's more than 13-year civil war.
But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces.
The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province.
0136b605eb676dd0: Singapore Civil Defence Force unveils robot that can extract, relocate electric vehicles involved in fires

SINGAPORE, Oct 28 — With electric vehicles (EV) gaining popularity, making up 57.6 per cent of all new car registrations in the first quarter of 2026, the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) is stepping up efforts to prepare for fire-related incidents.

The lifesaving force on Wednesday (October 28) unveiled its new Vehicle Extrication Robot (VXR) at the Singapore-International Disaster and Emergency Management Expo (SIDEX), held at the Singapore Expo.
Speaking at the event, Second Minister for Home Affairs Sim Ann pointed to SCDF’s Transformation 2030 vision, “Prepared, even for the unexpected”.

“The aim is not simply to respond better when emergencies occur, but to anticipate risks and strengthen capabilities before they are needed,” she highlighted, noting that the built environment has become more complex, alongside the emergence of new risks.
Sim noted that growing EV adoption can introduce new challenges for firefighters.
“Lithium-ion batteries can undergo thermal runaway, and affected vehicles may remain at risk of re-ignition even after a fire has been extinguished,” she pointed out.

Thermal runaway refers to a condition when an electrochemical cell increases its temperature through self-heating in an uncontrollable fashion and progresses when it is generating heat at a higher rate than can be dissipated.
And because the cells are densely packed, thermal runaway of one cell is likely to propagate and eventually set the whole battery on fire.
In a factsheet to the media on Wednesday, SCDF said that the risk of thermal runaway during EV battery fires require a holistic mitigation response.
“As affected EV batteries may remain at risk of re-ignition even after the fire has been extinguished, they need to be relocated to a safe area as quickly as possible,” said SCDF.

To this, the SCDF’s latest addition to its fleet of unmanned capabilities can be operated from up to 300 metres away, allowing firefighters to relocate an affected EV to a safe area once the fire has been extinguished.
The VXR is also equipped with an integrated water mist system that protects it from radiant heat.
Demonstrating its utility in a video, SCDF showed that an EV can still have high temperatures even after a fire has been put out.
In such cases, firefighters will deploy the VXR to tow the affected EV to another location. For example, if an affected vehicle is in an enclosed carpark, it will be relocated to an open space.
During the towing process, the VXR’s water mist system is activated to shield it from the risk of reignition.
Once in an open area, firefighters are then seen deploying other firefighting equipment, including unmanned firefighting machines, to cool down the vehicle.
The VXR will begin operational trials at Punggol Fire Station and Kallang Fire Station from October 2026 and April 2027 respectively. — AsiaOne
474f9da541a4c89a: KUALA LUMPUR: Artificial intelligence (AI) could sharply reduce the recruitment of young lawyers, former United Kingdom Supreme Court president Lord David Neuberger said.
He said AI's growing capabilities could reduce demand for junior lawyers, particularly in legal drafting and research.
"In the medium term, there is a real possibility that AI will cause a real fall-off in recruitment of young lawyers.

"By all accounts, AI can produce a first draft of a pleading, a letter of advice, or a piece of research, which can often be as good as that which would be produced by a young lawyer at the start of their career.
"And of course it will do so more quickly and cheaply.
"So, there would appear to be a real risk that recruitment of young lawyers will take a sharp dive," he said in his keynote address at the International Malaysia Law Conference 2026 here today.
Neuberger said accounts were already circulating in London suggesting the trend was emerging.
He warned that declining recruitment of junior lawyers could have long-term implications for the profession.
"If it does happen, it would not just be worrying for young lawyers, but it would raise the question of how do we get the next generation of experienced senior lawyers," he said.
However, Neuberger cautioned against firm predictions about AI's impact, noting that technological advances could also create new opportunities.
He said AI could make legal advice and representation more affordable, potentially increasing demand for legal services.
He also warned that excessive reliance on AI could weaken lawyers' critical thinking and analytical abilities.
Nevertheless, he acknowledged that AI could be a useful tool for lawyers and judges, provided its output was rigorously checked before being used in legal proceedings.
"I see nothing wrong in principle with lawyers or even judges using AI.
"Indeed, if it is a useful tool, we would need to have a very good reason not to use it," he said.
Neuberger said AI remained susceptible to inaccuracies and hallucinations, including generating legal authorities that did not exist.
He cited an incident in England in which the Court of Appeal publicly criticised an advocate for using AI-generated submissions containing fabricated court decisions.
He stressed that lawyers and judges must verify AI-generated information before incorporating it into legal advice, court submissions or judgments.
Looking further ahead, Neuberger said AI could eventually decide complex legal disputes, including questions of fact and law.
He also raised concerns about transparency and public acceptance if machines were allowed to make judicial decisions.

Neuberger said parties to legal disputes had a fundamental right to understand the reasons behind decisions affecting them, particularly when the consequences involved imprisonment, bankruptcy or the loss of their homes or children.
He added that the possibility that even AI developers might not understand how machines reached their conclusions posed a significant challenge to the administration of justice.

39cd73e1ccefb1b6: JERUSALEM: Israelis voted on Tuesday in their highest turnout for decades, with exit polls showing the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his rival are neck and neck.

Exit polls from the three mainstream Israeli television networks gave the two blocs around 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset -- well below the 61 needed to govern -- after initially giving an edge to the opposition led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats.

The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
It took Netanyahu 58 days to form his government after the previous election in November 2022.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20% of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.

Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for anyone that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said that an especially high Arab turnout "indicates a strong desire for partnership".
Eisenkot has not even entertained the possibility publicly, and Netanyahu relentlessly told Jewish voters in his campaign that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
"Bottom line, at the moment, it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results," Elovitz said.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, the prospect of a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.

Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on Oct 16 found that 55% of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.

This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.

A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.

The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

fe8c0cec7b382caf: JERUSALEM: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot each vowed on Wednesday to form a government after both came up short in the first election since the Oct 7, 2023 attack traumatised the country.

Voters turned out Tuesday in the highest numbers in decades to give their verdict on the divisive rule of Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to the Hamas attack.

Exit polls showed Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu's hard-right camp and both well away from the threshold for a majority in parliament.

The strongest gains came from Arab Israeli parties whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.
Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention centre after 3am, called for a "strong government of the right" and said that the "Jewish and Zionist majority must unite."
The 77-year-old prime minister was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.
Instead, he listed leaders Israel has killed under his orders and again hinted that he was ready for a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump, his close ally.
"Israel has a unique opportunity with our partner President Trump to forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran," Netanyahu said.
Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government.
"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Addressing Israel's security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him "a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust."
- 'PUBLIC HAS VOTED FOR CHANGE' -
Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu's views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive following Oct 7 that has reduced the territory to rubble.
But Eisenkot has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel and to rein in extremist settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.
After turnout of nearly 78 per cent, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work "swiftly" to form a government.
"The public has voted for change," Eisenkot said. "A worthy leader would accept the people's vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today."
The three mainstream Israeli television networks in exit polls gave the two blocs each around 51 seats – well below the 61 needed to govern – after initially giving an edge to the opposition.

Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 17 to 18 seats, a sharp gain, with some Israeli Arab communities reporting near-universal turnout driven by outrage to often derogatory rhetoric against them by Netanyahu's far-right allies.
Key Israeli Arab leader Mansour Abbas said he believed the right had "suffered a major loss" and was open to working with Eisenkot.
But Eisenkot said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers – and Netanyahu again suggested that a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.
Arab lawmakers could give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition. If not, Israel could head to new elections.
Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand who according to exit polls did not gain as much as many expected, warned Netanyahu against another option – a unity government with Eisenkot.
"It would be a terrible mistake," said Ben Gvir, who champions the expulsion of Palestinians and would likely be excluded from any unity government.
Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said Ben Gvir had succeeded in mobilising votes – of Israeli Arabs.
But he said: "Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn't mean Eisenkot won."
- DIVISIVE -

The election came as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Eisenkot is a political novice whose mild manner is the antithesis of the smooth-talking incumbent.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent.
Before voting, the 66-year-old Eisenkot paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.
Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial for their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Eisenkot's bloc.
"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.
The time to act is "now, or the country really won't survive anymore."--AFP

0769dddbcc271007: WHEN most people picture a stroke, they think of an older adult, often someone living with high blood pressure, diabetes or high cholesterol.
A stroke is rarely if ever associated with a child. Yet, a stroke can happen to young people of any age, from newborns to teenagers.

The Paediatric Protocols for Malaysian Hospitals, developed by the Health Ministry and Malaysian Paediatric Association, cites an estimated childhood stroke incidence of 2.5 to 13 cases per 100,000 children each year.
While uncommon compared with adult stroke, its rarity is part of the challenge, as sudden symptoms can easily be missed or mistaken for a more common childhood illness.
Sunway Medical Centre Velocity consultant paediatrician and paediatric neurologist Dr Tan Jen Ern explains that a paediatric stroke can occur at any age.
"Paediatric stroke is rare, but rarity does not mean it cannot happen."
The important thing is to recognise sudden neurological changes and seek emergency assessment promptly, he adds.
ACTING FAST
Part of what makes paediatric stroke difficult to identify is that children may not present the way adults do.
Unlike adults, children often cannot describe exactly what they are feeling, and many other childhood conditions can look like a stroke.
Add to that a general lack of awareness among both parents and healthcare professionals about the condition, and paediatric stroke can easily be overlooked, explains Dr Tan.

Warning signs can also look different depending on the child's age. In older children and teenagers, stroke can look much like it does in adults, with facial drooping, weakness on one side of the body or difficulty speaking.
In babies and toddlers, however, the signs can be far more subtle, such as seizures or difficulty feeding.
Because stroke is rarely expected in children, parents may wait to see if symptoms pass.

However, stroke remains a time-sensitive emergency regardless of age. Parents should note the time when the child was last known to be well, because the timing of symptoms can be important in determining emergency treatment options.
Calling an ambulance allows the emergency system to help coordinate the appropriate destination and facilitate transfer to a facility with stroke expertise, advises Dr Tan.

The nearest hospital is not always the one best equipped for an acute stroke. If the facility cannot promptly provide the necessary brain and vascular imaging or specialist assessment, the child may need to be referred or transferred.
That can mean additional time before the diagnosis is confirmed and before specialised treatment can be considered.
WHAT CAUSES A CHILDHOOD STROKE?
Unlike adults, children who have a stroke usually do not have lifestyle-related risk factors.

Paediatric stroke can instead be linked to heart disease, abnormalities of the blood vessels in the brain, blood disorders, infection or inflammation, trauma and certain genetic or metabolic conditions.
This means a child who appears completely healthy can still be affected.
"In most cases, these children have an underlying condition that has yet to be identified."

The most common underlying cause is an abnormality of the brain's blood vessels. Finding that cause requires a thorough investigation, including blood tests, screening for blood-clotting disorders (thrombophilia) where needed, heart tracing (ECG) and an ultrasound scan of the heart (echocardiogram), as well as a brain scan that also maps the blood vessels (MRI with MRA).
Initial treatment focuses on stabilising the child, controlling seizures and managing complications, with clot-preventing medications used depending on the cause.

For selected children who meet strict criteria, a minimally invasive procedure to remove the clot from a blocked artery (endovascular thrombectomy) may be considered with the necessary expertise. Identifying the cause also matters for the future, as Malaysia's paediatric protocol notes that 12 to 20 per cent of childhood arterial ischaemic strokes (strokes caused by a blocked artery) may recur.

"Recurrence risk is not the same for every child. An abnormality of the brain's arteries carries a higher risk. Treating the underlying cause can reduce that risk, alongside close follow-up with paediatric neurology and other relevant specialists."

For a child, stroke can affect far more than movement. A Malaysian study published last year followed 76 children for at least two years after their stroke. Around three in four recovered well enough to manage daily activities and showed good neurological recovery.
Even so, their overall quality of life remained noticeably lower than that of healthy Malaysian children, especially among those who developed learning difficulties.

A child may have a relatively good physical recovery but continue to experience difficulties with attention, processing speed, memory, learning, communication, emotional regulation, social participation or confidence. These can have a major effect on school, relationships and everyday life, explains Dr Tan. Some effects may only surface years later.
Dr Tan notes that a young child may seem to be recovering very well at first, only for difficulties to become more apparent as they start school and face greater learning and developmental demands.

This is why long-term follow-up matters, with rehabilitation forming a core part of care through physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, neuropsychological assessment and educational support.

3b277c187fb15465: KUALA LUMPUR: The government has yet to set a timeframe for resolving all outstanding 1Malaysia Development Bhd (1MDB) claims and completing asset recovery efforts.
Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan said the process depended on court decisions and enforcement actions locally and abroad.

"Currently, the government, through 1MDB, is intensifying efforts to negotiate compensation and recover assets and funds linked to 1MDB through legal action and asset recovery mechanisms, both locally and abroad," he said.

He was responding to Howard Lee Chuan How (PH-Ipoh Timor), who asked when the government expected to settle 1MDB's remaining net liabilities, estimated at RM20.1 billion, and how much it expected to recover from each claim.

Amir Hamzah said the government could not determine how much it would recover from individual claims, as estimates had to account for third-party rights, settlements, amounts already recovered and potential overlapping claims on the same funds.

"Although there is good potential for further recoveries based on the strength of the government's cases, the additional amounts recovered will not be sufficient to cover the losses incurred by the country," he said.
He said the government had paid RM42.5 billion as at Aug 31 to meet 1MDB's debts and related commitments, including principal, interest and other costs.

The remaining government-guaranteed Islamic Medium Term Note (IMTN) sukuk commitments stood at RM8.9 billion, comprising RM5 billion in principal and RM3.9 billion in interest, due by maturity in 2039.
This brought total liabilities, both paid and outstanding, to RM51.4 billion, he said.
"After deducting RM31.3 billion in recovered funds and assets, the government's net burden is estimated at RM20.1 billion, if there are no further recoveries," he said.

Amir Hamzah said the RM20.1 billion estimate represented losses borne by the government and the country as a result of the scandal, calculated by deducting compensation and recovered assets from the debt assumed by the government.
He said the amount eventually recoverable depended on court rulings, appeals, traceable assets and the ability to enforce orders, particularly overseas.
"As such, sums claimed or ordered by the courts cannot yet be considered amounts that will definitely be received," he said.
He said 2039 was the maturity year for the principal of IMTN sukuk under the current contractual schedule, but this was separate from the timeframe for resolving claims.
"Repaying sukuk holders does not mean all expenses borne by the government have been recovered.
"The government's priority is to meet its financial commitments on schedule while continuing to recover as much of the misappropriated funds as possible," he said.
8426c64d3afd2d58: SHAH ALAM: The service status of Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain at the Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) has been referred to the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) for legal advice.
The referral comes before any decision on whether to terminate or shorten his two-year tenure, which would require the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's consent.
Inspector-General of Police Tan Sri Mohd Khalid Ismail said the matter had also been referred to the Police Force Commission for further action.
Khalid said Shuhaily's assignment at MCBA was based on a two-year cadre secondment contract from the police, which had received the King's consent.
"We are referring this matter to the A-GC because Datuk Seri Shuhaily's assignment at MCBA is for a period of two years.
"It is like a contract, and this contract was made with the consent of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong.

"So, if anything happens involving suspension from duty and so on, our action will depend on the A-GC's advice. However, any decision on terminating the contract and so on must be submitted to the Yang di-Pertuan Agong," he said.
He was speaking to reporters after the 2026 National Conference on Bureaucratic Red Tape Reform, organised by the Malaysia Productivity Corporation (MPC).
Also present was Chief Secretary to the Government Tan Sri Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar.
Khalid said the AGC's advice was needed to ensure any action involving Shuhaily took into account the terms of his contract and the requirement to obtain the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's consent.

"His case has been referred to the A-GC for legal advice because he has a contract signed by the relevant parties for a period of about two years. The appointment was made with the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's consent.
"So, before taking any action, we need to obtain the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's consent again, whether to shorten his tenure or take other measures," he said.
Khalid said the matter would be referred back to the police for further action once the legal process and the process of obtaining the King's consent were completed.
"Once the process is completed, he will be returned to the police because Datuk Seri Shuhaily is still a serving police officer.
"Upon his return, I may provide further details on the necessary steps or follow-up action, God willing," he said.
Meanwhile, Shamsul Azri said any further action or arrangements concerning Shuhaily was left entirely to the Home Ministry and the Inspector-General of Police.
When asked whether the matter involved an investigation, Shamsul Azri said it should first be discussed with the police leadership.
6046a49cc8e8d4a5: KUALA LUMPUR: Dewan Rakyat hari ini diberitahu yang kertas siasatan berhubung dakwaan bekas perdana menteri Muhyiddin Yassin mempertahankan pemberian subsidi kerajaan kepada warga asing sudah dirujuk kepada Jabatan Peguam Negara (AGC).

Rosol mempersoalkan kelewatan siasatan terhadap dakwaan berkenaan dan bertanya sama ada tuduhan terhadap Muhyiddin (PN-Pagoh) itu benar.

Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim pada Ogos tahun lalu mengarahkan Suruhanjaya Komunikasi dan Multimedia Malaysia (SKMM) menyiasat dakwaan bahawa Muhyiddin mempertahankan pemberian subsidi kerajaan kepada warga asing.
