Bagaimanapun, katanya, platform terbabit akan membuat penilaian sendiri berdasarkan keperluan undang-undang serta garis panduan komuniti masing-masing.
Teo berkata AGC dan mahkamah pula memainkan peranan dalam proses pendakwaan jenayah, manakala individu yang didakwa tetap mempunyai hak untuk membela diri.
Terdahulu, beliau berkata MCMC mengemukakan 65,680 permintaan untuk menurunkan kandungan palsu dalam talian antara 1 Jan 2023 hingga 15 Okt 2026, dengan 56,304 daripadanya berjaya diturunkan.
fe021bd46ffec6c3: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 28 — Jury selection is expected to begin on Wednesday in Los Angeles for another landmark trial about the alleged harms of social media on young users, with Meta and, for the first time, Snap as defendants.

Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.
The cases — the first of which went to trial earlier this year in Los Angeles — have taken twists and turns.

Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier this year, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined $6 million penalty.
Meta said at the time that they “respectfully disagree” with the verdict.
Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.

Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August; that plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.

TikTok and YouTube were previously named as defendants in the new case but both companies reached settlement agreements with the plaintiffs, known by their initials SJ and KDB, before the start of the trial, their lawyers said.
Meta reached a settlement agreement with one of the plaintiffs, SJ, but not KDB, according to their lawyers.
A California state judge consolidated both cases into a single trial.
If no additional settlements are reached before opening statements kick off on November 4, the new trial will move forward with both Meta and Snap as defendants.
Star witnesses are expected to testify beginning mid-November including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri, and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion (RM102 billion) in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
A New Mexico jury previously found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of US$942 million.

In August, Meta agreed to pay more than US$18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys general several days into a trial held in California.
Part of that settlement hinged on YouTube and TikTok making similar changes to their own products, such as limiting daily screentime.
‘Addictive and problematic’

As regulators around the world grapple with reining in, or even banning, social media use for teens, American lawsuits have focused on allegations of addictive design and deceptive practices by social media companies.

Next month, lawyers for the two plaintiffs in Los Angeles — SJ and KDB — will argue that their clients were exposed to “addictive and problematic” social media apps when they started using them at 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.
SJ, a teen in Illinois, began to use Snapchat, the app created by Snap, compulsively and subsequently experienced mental health issues, an eating disorder and self harm, her lawyers claim.
KDB, now an 18-years-old from Mississippi, similarly developed compulsive use of both Meta and Snap, leading to worsening mental and physical health, according to her lawyers.
Meta has previously denied such claims.
“We will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits,” Meta told AFP in July.
Snap intends to argue that it is different from other apps like Meta’s Instagram and Facebook because of Snapchat’s focus on primarily being a messaging platform.

“We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement. — AFP

9967a5b2ecf8f951: KUALA LUMPUR: The investigation papers into a claim that former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin defended the distribution of government subsidies for foreigners has been referred to the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC), the Dewan Rakyat was told today.

"We have referred the case to the AGC and are awaiting its decision," she said in response to Rosol Wahid (PN-Hulu Terengganu).

"Until today, I am still waiting for an answer," he said.

In August last year, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim ordered the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) to investigate his claim that Muhyiddin had defended extending government subsidies to foreigners.
The Prime Minister’s Office said it acknowledged Muhyiddin’s denial of having made such remarks concerning targeted RON95 petrol subsidies.
Rosol also asked who had the authority to determine whether online content was false and what safeguards existed to prevent MCMC from suppressing legitimate criticism of the government.
He cited social media personalities, including Papagomo, whose content he alleged was removed and his electronic devices seized.
Teo said MCMC assessed complaints from government agencies, enforcement authorities and the public before requesting platforms to remove content suspected of breaching the law.
However, she said the platforms made their own assessments based on legal requirements and community guidelines.
Teo added that the AGC and courts played a role in criminal proceedings, while accused persons retained the right to defend themselves.
Earlier, she said MCMC submitted 65,680 requests for the removal of false online content between Jan 1, 2023 and Oct 15, 2026. Of these, 56,304 were successful.

a5512a74aa7207f7: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — The total fuel subsidy savings for this year will be finalised by year-end, taking into account actual transaction adjustments, weekly market prices, currency exchange rates, and verified consumption volumes.

Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan said that from a fiscal perspective, the implementation of BUDI95 is expected to generate total savings of between RM2.5 billion and RM4 billion annually.

“The savings are the result of the comprehensive implementation of targeted subsidies, which includes reducing leakage, such as benefits reaching non-citizens and ineligible consumer categories, as well as curbing expenditures that do not align with the government’s social protection objectives.

“The government will continue to ensure that these savings are repurposed to strengthen targeted assistance, such as the Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah, as well as other initiatives that provide direct benefits to the people,” he said.

He was replying to a question from Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh), who had asked the Finance Minister to state the actual amount of fuel subsidy savings for the year, in the Dewan Rakyat today.

Amir Hamzah stated that the government consistently adopts a responsive, data-driven approach, including continuous monitoring of developments in global energy supply and market prices, the nation’s fiscal position, and public feedback.

“Following more stable fuel supply conditions and current subsidy expenditure of approximately RM4 billion per month, the government is reinstating the BUDI95 eligibility limit to 300 litres per month, effective September 1, 2026.

“The previous adjustment from 300 litres to 200 litres was an initial, targeted measure to ensure the nation’s fuel supply remains secure amidst global supply uncertainties resulting from the conflict in West Asia,” he said. — Bernama
f845e66987086cb3: KOTA TINGGI, Oct 28 — A 41-year-old man suspected of hacking an elderly settler to death with an axe in Felda Lok Heng Selatan was remanded for seven days today to facilitate a murder investigation.
Pengerang Sessions Court Judge Hidayatul Syuhada Shamsudin granted the remand order, allowing police to detain the suspect until Nov 3 for investigations under Section 302 of the Penal Code.
Handcuffed and dressed in orange lock-up attire, the suspect arrived at the court complex at 9.45am under heavy police escort.

Johor police chief Datuk Ab Rahaman Arsad said yesterday that investigators arrested the man inside a nearby oil palm plantation on Tuesday morning, seizing a motorcycle alongside an axe believed to have been used in the fatal attack.
Background checks revealed that the suspect carries six prior criminal and drug-related records.

The arrest came after an alert at 7.56pm on Monday, when passers-by found 68-year-old settler lying in a pool of blood by the roadside in Felda Lok Heng Selatan with severe slash wounds to his head and arms. Medical personnel subsequently pronounced him dead.
Prior to the discovery of the body, alarmed residents reported seeing an axe-wielding man behaving aggressively along the village roadside.
2d6b416a62413648: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — A total of 25,464 participants in the MyLesen B2 Programme have completed their training and obtained their Class B2 Probationary Driving Licence (PDL), representing about 85 per cent of this year’s target.
The Ministry of Transport (MOT) said the government had allocated RM11.186 million to provide 30,000 places under the programme.
It said 30,660 individuals had been offered places and agreed to participate, exceeding the target by 2.2 per cent, while 28,785 had registered at driving institutes.

“Implementation in 11 states has reached 100 per cent, while the remaining participants in other states are completing their training and tests before the programme concludes on Oct 31, 2026,” the ministry said in a written parliamentary reply published on Parliament’s website.

The reply was in response to a question from Syerleena Abdul Rashid (PH-Bukit Bendera) on the process of obtaining a full driving licence under the MyLesen B2 Programme, from application to licence issuance, as well as the latest progress of the MyLesen B2 and MyLesen B2 Sekolah (MyB2S) programmes.

On the MyLesen B2 School (MyB2S) programme, which targets secondary school students from B40 (low-income) families, including those with special educational needs, the ministry said 50,642 students had been offered places.
Of these, 40,590 were undergoing training at driving institutes nationwide, while 30,648 had obtained their Learner’s Driving Licence (LDL).
A further 7,157 students had completed the process to obtain their Class B2 PDL.

“This figure is expected to continue rising, as many MyB2S participants are still undergoing training and practical tests,” the ministry said, adding that the government covered the costs of courses, training, the initial test and up to two repeat tests under the MyLesen B2 Programme.
The MOT said the process of obtaining a PDL typically took three to five months, depending on participants’ attendance, training schedules and commitment.
However, the ministry stressed that all assessment requirements must be met without exception, despite the programme being fully funded by the government.
“Our principle is simple — the government provides financial support, but competence and safety cannot be compromised,” it said.

The ministry said the initiatives went beyond providing financial assistance to obtain a driving licence, as they also aimed to ensure that young people and those from B40 families received formal training, understood road traffic laws and acquired the basic skills needed to ride safely on public roads. — Bernama
aad5e7b25bfa7c50: PETALING JAYA: The investigation into an alleged axe attack on a teacher by a 16-year-old at a private school in Kuching has been completed, with police submitting the investigation papers to the deputy public prosecutor yesterday.

Sarawak acting police commissioner Saifullizan Ishak said further decisions on the case would depend on the prosecution’s review of the probe papers and a forensic psychiatric report on the suspect, Harian Metro reported.

"The forensic psychiatric report is important for determining the suspect’s mental state at the time of the incident, including whether he acted consciously or was out of control," he told a press conference at the Sarawak police headquarters in Kuching.
Saifullizan said preliminary investigations found that the suspect bought the axe online. An analysis of his mobile phone and computer is ongoing to obtain information related to the Oct 21 incident.
Saifullizan said the teenager was still receiving treatment in hospital while undergoing psychiatric and medical assessments.
He said police found no evidence that the teenager was bullied leading up to the incident.

On claims that the teenager might have been influenced by online games or certain content, Saifullizan said the matter was still under investigation and police would not draw conclusions without credible evidence.
The 42-year-old teacher sustained a cut to her left hand, but the injury did not involve any muscles or bones. She was discharged after receiving treatment at a private hospital in Kuching.
Saifullizan said police had recorded statements from 38 witnesses, including students, teachers, security guards, medical experts and the suspect’s parents.
The 16-year-old student was arrested following the incident which he allegedly livestreamed on social media. He was also reportedly carrying firecrackers.
The case was probed for voluntarily causing hurt with dangerous weapons and handling explosives.
c8764d3cd1c9b3b2: SINGAPORE, Oct 28 — Three men, believed to be members of a transnational scam syndicate, were arrested between October 26 and 27 for their alleged involvement in using stolen debit and credit card details to commit payment fraud across Singapore.
The police said on Tuesday (October 27) night that they were alerted to a case at a retail establishment on Rochor Canal Road on Monday night.
A 36-year-old man had earlier bought two graphics cards, valued at over S$2,700 (RM8,600), from a retail store using a mobile wallet.
He later returned to the store about an hour later and attempted to buy more such components valued at over S$4,000.
The store staff alerted security officers on duty after becoming suspicious of the man's behaviour. They detained him and called the police.

Police said preliminary investigations revealed that he had received instructions through mobile application to carry out high-end product purchases including graphics cards and other IT components using a mobile wallet.
After making the purchase, he allegedly handed over the fraudulently obtained items to his accomplices, who were waiting in a vehicle, before returning to the store again.

The two accomplices, aged 25 and 27, were identified by officers from the Central Police Division through follow-up investigations and with the aid of images from closed-circuit television and police cameras.
By then, the duo had left the location in a rental vehicle, but they were separately arrested in the transit area of Changi Airport on Tuesday.
Further investigations revealed that the two men were also allegedly involved in at least one other case of payment fraud at another store, the police said.
Following their arrest, GeForce RTX 5070 graphics cards, an iPhone 18 Pro Max, and several other mobile phones in their possession were seized as case exhibits.
The three men will be charged in court on October 28 with abetment of conspiracy to cheat.
If found guilty of the said offence, they could each face jail of up to 10 years and a fine.
The police warned would-be perpetrators that it is a serious offence to defraud retailers, adding that they take a serious view against anybody who may be involved in scams and frauds.

Members of the public are also advised to be prudent when making online payments using their card details, to visit only reliable websites for online shopping, to safeguard their card details and not to disclose sensitive banking information with anyone.
Those whose credit/debit cards are lost or stolen should immediately call their card-issuing bank. — AsiaOne
85864ace8718cb50: BRUSSELS: President Donald Trump may be facing a political pounding at the US midterm elections next month -- but in Europe expectations are low that a big Democrat win would change much.
From the battlefields of Ukraine to the boardrooms of Europe, Trump has sent multiple shockwaves across the continent since returning to power last year.
During a head-spinning 22 months, the mercurial leader has turned spectacularly on Kyiv, imposed tariffs on allies and threatened to take Greenland.
Ahead of the Nov 3 polls it looks like American voters could punish Trump's Republican party and hand control of one or both of the US House of Representatives or Senate to the Democrats.
But while the hope may be that Trump could be reined in by a hostile Congress, multiple officials at the EU and Nato told AFP they doubt a big loss would muzzle him on the international stage.
"We don't think the unpredictability is going to change," said one senior EU diplomat.
Publicly the European Union is keeping its cards close to its chest.
"We will not comment on any elections in the EU or abroad. Let's wait for those and we'll see where it goes," said European Commission spokeswoman Paula Pinho.
Behind closed doors as well, officials say that the midterms are not featuring much in the bloc's internal discussions.

"I suspect because a) it is difficult to really predict the result, b) one wouldn't want to get too high hopes for change and c) not sure how much even a Democratic wave would impact foreign policy issues," said a second senior EU diplomat.
Ukraine, tariffs
Ahead of the midterms, Trump has rattled Europe by yet again lashing out at Ukraine and cosying up to Russia as Washington has renewed its push to end the fighting.
While a Democrat win could usher in a more vocal pro-Kyiv majority in Congress, the EU is not expecting US support for Ukraine to ramp up again.
Officials in Brussels say they are focused on plugging a 70-billion-euro hole in Kyiv's finances next year.
And while they're pushing other countries like Britain, Canada and Japan to do more, they are certainly not counting on the US.
Meanwhile, there is equally little optimism for any major reversal on the tariffs Trump has slapped on Europe.
Diplomats and officials point out that it took months to get Democrat President Joe Biden to roll back tariffs on EU steel after Trump's first term -- and even then limitations remained.
In a recent poll from the Washington-based Council on Foreign Relations, only one quarter of Americans backed removing all the tariffs on the EU.
US forces in Europe?
At Nato the story is much the same.
European allies are nervously waiting for the results of a Pentagon review of US forces on the continent that looks set to be unveiled in December.
The widespread expectation is that it will see the US scale back its deployments, although the hope is the cuts will not be too severe.
Multiple diplomats at Nato said they didn't envision the midterms having an impact on the review.

While a changed Congress could see US lawmakers more outspoken in support of the alliance, the direction of travel is already set with Europe stepping up efforts to take more responsibility for its defence.
"Whatever the outcome, we'll keep going," said one European diplomat.
Trump unleashed?
There is also a nagging fear that things could get worse after the midterms.
If Republicans cling on it could embolden Trump, meanwhile if they lose, he could seek to distract from his woes at home by stirring up things abroad.
"We have a history in America of presidents who get in trouble domestically turning more to the international stage," said Bruce Stokes, a visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund think tank.
From an escalation in the Iran war to a more concerted push on Ukraine, there are numerous ways the White House can keep worrying Europe.
"Trump has demonstrated they can't stand not to be the centre of attention," said Stokes.
"If that means he needs to do more on the world stage, positively or negatively, that may be what ends up happening."
10dc14716456714d: SAN FRANCISCO: Investors have long treated the US dollar as a refuge when markets fall, but foreign money chasing returns from the AI boom could weaken that safe-haven role if the trade unwinds.

Foreign capital has poured in to US mega-cap equities, hyperscaler corporate bonds and power-grid infrastructure. That has made the dollar an increasingly crowded bet on American exceptionalism, backed by faster growth, higher yields and persistent foreign demand for US assets.

But if the AI narrative stumbles, the dollar's safe-haven status could collide with its growing role as a risk-sensitive asset owned increasingly by price-sensitive investors. A sustained selloff in stocks could lead investors to sell US assets, potentially drowning out the safe-haven demand for the currency.
If the AI trade unwinds, "it's not as clear the dollar benefits in the same way it would have done in the past," said Dominic Bunning, head of G10 FX strategy at Nomura.
Storm warning on forex flows

Last week offered an early warning. When AI valuations came under pressure, haven flows favoured the Japanese yen and Swiss franc over the dollar. The greenback managed to eke out modest gains against the euro, mainly due to the single currency being dented by concerns over French civil unrest.
"The relationship between the AI trade and the dollar has become much more visible when the AI trade comes under scrutiny," said Kevin Ford, lead FX and macro strategist at Convera.

Foreign flows into US equities are at a record, while foreign direct investment has lagged. As a result, much of the capital is coming from institutional allocators that may buy or sell when they reassess US growth, rates, or tech valuations.

Erik Nelson, global head of FX strategy at Wells Fargo, likens these allocations to the "hot money" flows that dominate emerging markets. The AI boom has reinforced expectations of stronger US growth, firmer inflation and higher rates, lifting the dollar alongside Treasury yields, analysts said.
"The whole AI trade caused US rates to reprice higher, which has caused the dollar to rally," said Noah Buffam, FX strategist at CIBC Capital Markets.
If returns disappoint, an unwind could hit equities, credit and rates, leaving the dollar vulnerable on three fronts.

Weaker growth could force the Federal Reserve to cut rates, eroding the dollar's yield advantage. Slower domestic investment would puncture the exceptionalism narrative. And fading institutional demand for US corporate bonds and equities would weaken a major source of structural support.
So far, investors have been willing to buy dips, suggesting that any sustained weakness could be a process taking months or years.
The dotcom lesson

An equity route alone would not automatically sink the dollar, Nelson said. After the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000, the dollar stayed firm for nearly two years before cracking when US credit markets came under stress following collapses such as WorldCom's and due to other factors such as a recovery in global growth.

But the AI buildout is more US-centric. Nelson said the real trade-weighted dollar has stayed above its long-run average, measured since 1973, for 12 consecutive years, the longest stretch on record. Foreign inflows are also more concentrated in equities and corporate bonds than in 2000, while foreign direct investment is weaker.

If infrastructure investments fail to pay off, credit spreads could widen, forcing AI companies to curb capital spending. That could ripple through the economy, softening demand for industrial equipment, hardware and energy.

Concerns about riskier parts of the AI universe, such as heavily indebted neocloud companies including Core Weav have already widened credit default swap spreads sharply in recent weeks, adding to pressure on stocks.
"We can see this fraying around the edges when we look at credit default swaps," said Shaun Osborne, chief FX strategist at Scotiabank.
Washington also runs a large fiscal deficit now, compared with a surplus near the 2000 tech peak. That leaves less room for counter-cyclical stimulus without unsettling debt markets.
Sensitivity under stress

For Nelson, the key signal is not simply whether US tech shares fall, but whether stress becomes a US-specific credit and growth problem that can also change expectations for Fed policy. In such a scenario the yen would likely benefit at the dollar's expense, a shift that could have further ramifications for markets that would already likely be under stress.

That is not to say a dollar decline is a foregone conclusion. A shock severe enough to trigger a scramble for dollar funding could initially strengthen the dollar. In 2008 and March 2020, investors rushed to obtain dollars to meet dollar-denominated liabilities, creating a powerful but temporary bid.

In any case, some investors believe the dollar is back on the table as a major risk factor in the most significant way since the rout caused by US President Donald Trump's announcement of sweeping tariffs in April 2025.

"The sensitivity of global investors to a large re-rating or selloff in the dollar is substantial," Nelson said. "As we go into '27, it's a vulnerability for the dollar that I think is worth watching.”
8587d08519d20e70: Korean memory-maker SK Hynix has predicted memory shortages will persist until at least the year 2030 and says that will help it to boost its already exceptional revenue and profits to new levels.

In remarks published on Wednesday alongside its quarterly results, the company offered its belief that “a virtuous cycle has taken hold in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue generation in areas such as software development, customer service, and search lead to greater AI adoption, which in turn drives increased investment in infrastructure.”

SK Hynix thinks this is great news, because it means more buyers are entering the market for AI infrastructure, including “general enterprises” and nations building sovereign infrastructure. In coming years, the company sees even more demand for memory coming from autonomous cars and the growing robotics market.
While the company is working hard to build more factories and get them working, execs admitted it can’t do that fast enough to meet demand.

“The company assessed that supply … is not keeping pace with the growth of the market,” SK Hynix told investors. “Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.”

It gets worse. SK Hynix has 14 long-term deals with 14 big buyers, who will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers” and give it “a structure that secures stable profitability while allowing flexible responses to market changes.”

Those deals helped SK Hynix to record quarterly revenue of ₩104.6 trillion ($78.1 billion), up 328 percent year-over-year and 32 percent quarter-over-quarter. Operating profit came in at ₩87.68 trillion ($62.8 billion), up 486 percent year over year.
The company told investors it’s not done yet, outlining plans to expand production and emphasize lucrative products that will “scale up revenue and profit one step further next year.”

Doing so will likely dent profits elsewhere, because on the company’s earnings call, chief financial officer Kim Woo-hyun predicted “shipment volumes for PCs and mobile devices are expected to decrease due to cost burdens from rising memory prices and supply shortages.”
The company also outlined some of its future plans, among them:
Increasing HBM4 production, which it believes will “surpass HBM3E in both shipment volume and revenue in the fourth quarter and … establish itself as a mainstream product.”
“Rapidly” increasing the portion of its 10nm-class 6th generation (1c) process technology and expand sales of DDR5 and LPDDR5 SOCAMM for AI servers.
Developing NAND “into a core solution that enhances the throughput and economic efficiency of AI services, based on HBF and system optimization technologies.”

Investors liked what they heard, with some apparently seeing the memory-maker’s outlook as suggesting the AI boom won’t sputter out any time soon and sent the company’s share price up by about three percent in after-hours trading. ®
51b5f9397cd39f8e: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — A total of 88 local authorities (PBTs) nationwide have received recognition under the Malaysia Smart City Rating since its introduction in 2023.

The Ministry of Housing and Local Government (KPKT), in a statement today, said the achievement reflected progress in implementing the national smart city agenda to improve service delivery efficiency, urban sustainability and public well-being through technology and innovation.

“This recognition reflects the progress made by local authorities in adopting a smart city approach based on established indicators, while encouraging continuous improvements in management and service delivery to the public,” the ministry said.

The ministry said 28 local authorities had been approved to receive new recognition this year based on the Malaysia Standard (MS) ISO 37122:2019, Sustainable Cities and Communities – Indicators for Smart Cities.
Of these, one local authority achieved Level 3: Leading Smart City; nine achieved Level 2: Developing Smart City; and 18 achieved Level 1: Smart City Early Adopter.
KPKT said the development was confirmed at the 2026 National Smart City Council (MBPN) meeting chaired by Housing and Local Government Minister Nga Kor Ming yesterday.

“KPKT will continue to strengthen the smart city agenda through close cooperation between the federal government, state governments, local authorities and the private sector to ensure that urban development benefits the people, in line with Malaysia’s aspiration to become a Smart Nation by 2040,” he said. — Bernama
7a255db590dc3f86: MUMBAI, Oct 28 — Shares in India’s Jio Platforms surged more than 21 per cent on its market debut Wednesday, after raising more than $3 billion (RM12.2 billion) in the country’s biggest initial public offering.

The company, home to India’s biggest wireless operator and which is the digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, opened at 1,358 rupees on the National Stock Exchange — well up from its 1,119-rupee issue price.
Launched a decade ago, Jio’s wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.

With more than 530 million subscribers, the firm currently makes most of its money from telecoms, but has expanded in recent years into newer areas including digital services and artificial intelligence.
The listing, one of the most anticipated this year, attracted robust demand last week with the IPO being 22 times oversubscribed.

“In our first 10 years, we democratised data... In our next 10, we want to democratise every technology that can transform Indian lives,” Akash Ambani, managing director of Jio Platforms and Mukesh’s eldest son, said at the listing ceremony in financial capital Mumbai.
“AI, cloud, connected devices, connectivity even from space and digital services not yet imagined.”
Analysts at Nomura, who initiated coverage on the stock on Wednesday, said the company’s focus for Jio had shifted “from adding users to earning more from each customer”.
“We believe the heavy 5G investment cycle is largely behind for Jio... freeing up significant cash flow,” they said.
Experts say Jio is key to Reliance’s strategy to evolve beyond its traditional oil business and the touchstone of its future tech ambitions.

Local media have reported that it is considering a low-orbit satellite constellation to provide internet services from space — a venture that would see it compete with Elon Musk’s Starlink, which has been trying for years to launch in India.

The world’s richest man accused unnamed Indian “oligarchs” this month of preventing Starlink’s rollout in the country, and referred to the Reliance chairman as “Prime Minister Ambani” and the “real boss of India”.
Reliance responded by noting that it had never “feared competition” and welcomed offerings from rivals in satellite communications, including Starlink.
While Jio has expanded beyond its telecom roots, experts have cautioned investors that it will take time for its efforts to bear fruit.
Monetisation of newer digital services are “still to be demonstrated at scale”, analysts at financial services firm Motilal Oswal noted earlier this month. — AFP

a2f2c597025154db: HONG KONG, Oct 28 — Technology firms surged across Asia on Wednesday after blockbuster earnings from chip giant SK hynix helped boost optimism in the AI trade ahead of results from Wall Street titans Microsoft and Alphabet.
Oil prices rose as investors kept tabs on Israel’s election results, which could determine the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s war against Iran.
After a slight wobble this month in the tech realm caused by fresh worries about huge investment spending, profitability and company finances, AI-linked firms were back on the front foot.

SK hynix, which has been at the forefront of the chip boom, said Wednesday that third-quarter operating profit soared 632 per cent to US$62.8 billion (RM256.40 billion) thanks to explosive demand for its advanced semiconductors.
The firm said it had now posted record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters.

“While Wall Street argues over whether the AI arms race can keep financing itself, SK hynix has just reminded the market that somebody on the other side of all that capex is receiving the cheque,” wrote Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

The reading added to optimism surrounding the sector after Anthropic, the mother company for Claude AI, said Monday in its IPO filing that first-half revenue surged about 1,300 per cent and flagged heavy capital spending ahead.
That was followed Tuesday by Broadcom’s announcing jointly with Citi, Blackstone and Morgan Stanley a US$63 billion financing structure to build new capacity for Anthropic.

“The AI trade has undoubtedly received a healthy shot in the arm from Anthropic’s... filing, with its incredible revenue growth, improving compute economics and substantial commitments to future infrastructure investment reinforcing the longer-term opportunity across the AI supply chain,” said Pepperstone’s Chris Weston.

Shares in SK hynix soared almost nine per cent Wednesday and South Korean rival Samsung, which reports Thursday, added more than eight per cent. That pushed Seoul’s Kospi index up more than six per cent.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed more than one per cent, with chipmaker Kioxia soaring more than 10 per cent, while Advantest gained three per cent and Tokyo Electron four per cent.
Taipei was pulled sharply higher thanks to chipmaker TSMC’s strong performance, while Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington were also well up.
The gains tracked advances in New York, where the Nasdaq added more than one per cent.
Microsoft and Alphabet are due to report later in the day, while Amazon, Apple and Intel follow on Thursday.
However, traders are also awaiting the Federal Reserve’s policy decision Wednesday.

While it is expected to stand pat after last month’s hike, its post-meeting statement and comments from boss Kevin Warsh will be pored over for clues about its future plans. Markets expect a hike in December.
Crude prices jumped more than one per cent as results from Israel’s general election rolled in.

While polls appeared to show Netanyahu’s governing Likud and the opposition neck and neck, the prime minister vowed to form a new coalition, adding that he could work with US President Donald Trump to eliminate the “existential threat” posed by Iran.
His comments came after opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said the country had chosen change and that he would seek to form a new administration. — AFP
212e4d5ea2cabae8: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Malaysia has called for a stronger, more coordinated and effective regional disaster response capability among Asean member states to address increasingly complex and interconnected threats facing the region.

Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said no Asean member state, regardless of its resources, could address these challenges entirely on its own, underscoring the need for closer regional cooperation and collective preparedness.

“In this regard, Malaysia believes that Asean must work towards building a stronger, more coordinated and effective regional disaster response capability,” he said in his opening remarks at the 20th Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM), being held in Cebu, the Philippines, today and tomorrow.
The text of his speech was made available to Bernama.

He said non-traditional threats were no longer distant possibilities but had become real, recurring and increasingly difficult to ignore, requiring Asean to strengthen its ability to prevent, prepare for and respond to crises.
Mohamed Khaled said the response must begin with more proactive and coordinated initiatives to strengthen communities’ ability to prepare for, withstand and recover from such shocks.
He also stressed the importance of developing strong local and regional capacity to ensure an effective response when disasters strike.

Malaysia’s call builds on existing regional mechanisms, including the Asean Militaries Ready Group on Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (AMRG on HADR), which provides a framework for coordinating military assistance and facilitating the deployment of military assets to disaster-affected areas.
Mohamed Khaled cited Asean’s response to the earthquake in Myanmar last year as an example of the mechanism’s role in regional disaster relief efforts.

“We must now build upon these foundations to strengthen operational readiness, improve coordination and ensure that our armed forces can respond swiftly and effectively when disasters strike,” he said.
He said the need for stronger cooperation extended beyond disaster response, as Asean faced greater strategic competition, uncertainty and rapidly evolving security threats.
“As the ADMM enters its third decade, we must be prepared to do more than confront new threats with old approaches,” he said.

Mohamed Khaled said greater collective preparedness, stronger coordination and sustained investment in capabilities were necessary to ensure defence cooperation delivered tangible benefits to the people.

He said Asean’s peace and stability should never be taken for granted, adding that the region’s strength rested on mutual trust, constructive management of differences and a shared commitment to regional interests.

“Malaysia remains firmly committed to strengthening the ADMM, upholding Asean Centrality, and building a more secure and resilient regional community,” he said, adding that ADMM has become an important platform for practical defence cooperation, confidence-building and collective responses to shared security challenges. — Bernama

719d5abf83827800: JERUSALEM, Oct 28 — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot each vowed on Wednesday to form a government after both came up short in the first election since the October 7, 2023 attack traumatised the country.

Voters turned out Tuesday in the highest numbers in decades to give their verdict on the divisive rule of Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to the Hamas attack.

Exit polls showed Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu’s hard-right camp and both well away from the threshold for a majority in parliament.

The strongest gains came from Arab Israeli parties whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.

Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention centre after 3am (0100 GMT), called for a “strong government of the right” and said that the “Jewish and Zionist majority must unite”.
The 77-year-old prime minister was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.
Instead, he listed leaders Israel has killed under his orders and again hinted that he was ready for a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump, his close ally.
“Israel has a unique opportunity with our partner President Trump to forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran,” Netanyahu said.
Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government.
“Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Addressing Israel’s security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him “a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust”.
‘Public has voted for change’
Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu’s views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive following October 7 that has reduced the territory to rubble.
But Eisenkot has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel and to rein in extremist settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.
After turnout of nearly 78 per cent, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work “swiftly” to form a government.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
The three mainstream Israeli television networks in exit polls gave the two blocs each around 51 seats — well below the 61 needed to govern — after initially giving an edge to the opposition.

Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 17 to 18 seats, a sharp gain, with some Israeli Arab communities reporting near-universal turnout driven by outrage to often derogatory rhetoric against them by Netanyahu’s far-right allies.
Key Israeli Arab leader Mansour Abbas said he believed the right had “suffered a major loss” and was open to working with Eisenkot.
But Eisenkot said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers — and Netanyahu again suggested that a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.
Arab lawmakers could give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition. If not, Israel could head to new elections.
Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand who according to exit polls did not gain as much as many expected, warned Netanyahu against another option — a unity government with Eisenkot.
“It would be a terrible mistake,” said Ben Gvir, who champions the expulsion of Palestinians and would likely be excluded from any unity government.
Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said Ben Gvir had succeeded in mobilising votes — of Israeli Arabs.
But he said: “Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn’t mean Eisenkot won.”
Divisive

The election came as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Eisenkot is a political novice whose mild manner is the antithesis of the smooth-talking incumbent.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent.
Before voting, the 66-year-old Eisenkot paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.
Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial for their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.
“The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad,” she said.
The time to act is “now, or the country really won’t survive anymore”. — AFP

Within the same period, MCMC investigated 546 cases involving fake content under Section 233 of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998.
Teo said 34 cases were issued compounds amounting to RM1.72 million, 390 cases were classified as ‘no further action’, and 29 cases remain under active investigation.
Nine cases were prosecuted in court, with a dozen concluded resulting in total fines of RM75,500, the deputy minister added.

Teo was responding to Datuk Rosol Wahid (PN-Hulu Terengganu), who also questioned if action was taken against Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim for alleging his predecessor Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin supported foreign nationals to use subsidised fuel.
Anwar made the allegation in August last year and directed the MCMC to investigate Muhyiddin, who denied and demanded Anwar retract the remark and apologise.
Teo said the case had been relayed to the Attorney General’s Chambers.
“We have referred the case to the AGC, so we are still waiting for a decision from the AGC.”
9e57b3c7cb0d7eb2: The crack of a bat accompanied by a roar from the crowd can capture a baseball fan’s attention, even if they miss seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also perceive the world around us by listening to it.  To improve artificial perception, MIT Professor Paris Smaragdis SM ’97, PhD ’01 seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans. A machine with super-human hearing could rapidly pinpoint the location of a traffic accident by listening for squealing tires and crunching metal, or identify when an industrial drill might break while it is boring through dense bedrock to dig a geothermal well. “I like to say that I do the same thing the computer vision folks do, but instead I do it for hearing,” says Smaragdis, a professor with joint appointments in the Music and Theatre Arts program of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences, and the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science in the School of Engineering and the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing.  His research group explores areas like machine learning for sound source separation, smart devices that can augment the audio surroundings of humans, and better tools to help people understand, manipulate, analyze, and create music. “Having had a musical background, I’ve been interested in examining these ideas. What does it take to make machines understand sound? There is a huge domain of applications for machines that can listen,” says Smaragdis, who joined MIT in 2025. A musical prelude Smaragdis, who grew up in Greece, began playing classical guitar at a young age. He enjoyed playing traditional pieces but reached a turning point in his musical journey when his father brought home a small synthesizer. “That little synthesizer had a function that allowed you to make your own sounds, and I became completely captivated by the possibilities,” he says. Synthesizers were taking a more prominent place in pop music during the 1980s, adding to his fascination with the technology. As he advanced through school, Smaragdis wanted to study music made with synthesizers. But this was not an educational path offered by the more traditional European conservatories at the time. Instead, he enrolled at Berklee College of Music in Boston, into a program where he could explore the use of computers and synthesizers to shape and manipulate sound. “With computers and synthesizers, I could make new sounds that have never been heard before,” he says. At the same time, Smaragdis became immersed in jazz fusion. He declared bass as his major at Berklee since it would allow him more opportunities to play with jazz ensembles. “I found the bass to be sonically more interesting than the guitar. It was a more unexplored domain, and I’ve always gravitated toward unexplored domains,” he says. That interest in the unexplored carried over into his coursework. He and mentor Richard Boulanger, a professor of electronic production and design, created new tools to help people use computers to write, produce, and enhance music.  Through his studies at Berklee, Smaragdis embarked on a collaborative project with Professor Barry Vercoe (who passed away in 2025) at the MIT Media Lab to create software synthesizers for music creation. Building on that project, Smaragdis pursued graduate studies in Vercoe’s group, where he completed his master’s degree and PhD, followed by a postdoc. “In the Media Lab, I got exposed more to the computer part of computer music. That’s where my attention shifted a bit. Now I really wanted to make computers that could understand sound,” he says. Tuning in to unexplored domains At that time, many students in the Media Lab were using signal processing techniques to help machines handle sound. Smaragdis chose a less explored approach — machine learning — to separate himself from the pack. He found that training machine-learning models to understand sound offered advantages that couldn’t be attained with traditional signal processing techniques. “Over time, it became really clear to me that we need to teach computers how to listen. We can’t just tell them how to listen. If anything, we don’t even know how we humans listen,” he says. “We don’t have a vocabulary to explain what it means to listen, or how to tell the difference between a cat’s meow and the sound of a violin.” After finishing his postdoc, Smaragdis began a career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, where he worked on artificial intelligence systems that could scan video soundtracks and understand what is happening on screen.  “What if you record an entire soccer game, but you only want to watch the highlights? In computer vision, it is very difficult to identify what a highlight is. But on the other hand, if you only listen to the sounds, then when the crowd goes crazy you would know that something interesting is happening,” he says. That system was eventually incorporated into electronic devices, including a personal video recording system Mitsubishi was developing at the time, and into traffic monitoring systems and cell phones. Smaragdis later joined Adobe, where he created the audio research team that built user-friendly tools to help artists, musicians, and producers manipulate sound without needing a lot of expertise. “As we did that work, I kept coming up with deeper technical problems that needed to be resolved. I jumped into academia to address that itch,” he says. Smaragdis joined the faculty at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he and his group incorporated the latest machine-learning techniques into audio-processing systems. One of the technologies they developed utilized neural networks for separating individual sounds from audio mixtures. That project caught the attention of the team working on the 2021 documentary mini-series “The Beatles: Get Back.” The production team enlisted Smaragdis to help clean up some archival Beatles recordings. “That was a very different way of audio processing than what I was doing in academia. Now, I had to do something that sounded good but didn’t necessarily have to look good on paper. We didn’t have a formula we could optimize,” he says. Every recording involved different challenges. For instance, in one clip John Lennon was playing music while Paul McCartney was horsing around, reading headlines from newspapers and making fun of George Harrison. “We were trying to come up with a technological solution that could help us do everything, as opposed to addressing each problem on its own,” he says. His contributions helped the team win an Emmy Award for sound editing for a nonfiction or reality program, in 2022. A concerted effort After 15 years at the University of Illinois, Smaragdis decided to join the faculty at MIT to tackle the thorny, interdisciplinary problems that were emerging in the field.  His group now focuses on two main areas. For one, they develop systems that make computers more useful tools for musicians.  One project in this area is enabling machines to understand how to listen to music, so they can provide constructive feedback to musicians. “We want to enhance the toolbox a musician has. We don’t want to use computers to replace musicians,” he says. On the other side, his group focuses on the fundamental tools scientists and artists alike can use to process, analyze, and manipulate audio. For instance, his team has recently been exploring algorithms that allow sophisticated signal processing where traditional frames of reference, such as sampling rates, frame sizes, or context-windows, are not fixed — or even defined.  That implies different computational structures that are yet unexplored, despite their potential for more efficient processing, Smaragdis says. “That requires rethinking a lot of the basics, but once you have that ability, you can start getting much more flexible and more powerful systems,” he adds. They also explore ways to incorporate the latest techniques, like large language models, into speech recognition and audio enhancement. “AI is an immensely powerful tool, but I don’t think we have found the ideal way to use it for sound and music yet,” he says. He also enjoys mentoring students and helping them materialize their visions for research projects. Since few of his students have experience using computation in sound, he emphasizes hands-on lessons so they see and hear how to transform equations into something tangible. Smaragdis still feels a thrill from making music, whether with a computer or a more traditional instrument. Off campus, he tries to play jazz bass whenever he can find the time, and enjoys exploring the rich musical community of Boston with his wife and 15-year-old son. Outside the musical realm, he plays and coaches underwater hockey — a sport where players wear diving masks and use sticks to push a heavy puck across the bottom of a pool toward their opponent’s goal. He coached the underwater hockey team at the University of Illinois, and is hoping to revive the MIT underwater hockey club soon and start hosting tournaments on campus. While underwater hockey may be a lesser-known sport, it fits with Smaragdis’ lifelong interest in pursuing the underexplored. “I’ve always like doing things that were different from what everyone else was doing. If you can create a new sound that no one has heard before, what does that mean about your ability to create new things? I still find these questions completely fascinating,” he says.
c40e451ead73ac22: BATTICALOA: Tired but resolute, dozens of Tamil cattle farmers have held a round-the-clock vigil for almost three years in eastern Sri Lanka, protesting what they call land "theft".
At shift change, farmers exchange news before settling beneath a tarpaulin beside photographs of the bloodied bodies of their dead cows.

"They have been shooting our cattle, threatening us, assaulting us, and spraying pesticides or poison on the pasture lands where our cattle graze," said Seenithamby Thiyagarajah, president of the local farmers' association, detailing the push his community felt from recipients of a state-funded program that was driving them off their land.
"Over 5,700 cows have been destroyed like this. Even after complaining numerous times to the police and all relevant places, we received no resolution."
The alleged perpetrators are farmers who have benefited from the state-funded Mahaweli development scheme.
Most are Sinhalese, the country's majority ethnic group, settling on land claimed by the largely Hindu Tamil minority, which makes up about 12% of the population.
The government denied any forcible attempts to remove people from their land.
Sri Lanka's 1983-2009 civil war between government forces and Tamil separatists killed more than 100,000 people, according to the United Nations.
Nearly two decades later, land disputes continue to fuel ethnic grievances.
'You must leave'

Thiyagarajah says settlers aided by the scheme have encroached on grazing land used by the roughly 1,000 cattle farmers he represents. Courts have repeatedly ordered the eviction of the scheme-backed settler farmers, he said.
"Things are peaceful, for a while," he said. "But then the illegal cultivators entered again, ruining our land and destroying our cattle."
Other communities are also fighting to reclaim land.
Ambalavar Nallathambi Velayutham, 64, an Indigenous community leader, wants his rice fields back.
Armed with renewed land deeds renewed with local authorities, Velayutham and neighbours in Kunjankulam returned to farming fields they had abandoned during the war.
Forest Department officials then told them the land was a reserve, according to Velayutham.
"We said; 'This land belonged to our ancestors'. They replied, 'That won't do. You must leave.'"
Fearing reprisals, most villagers abandoned their efforts.
One night, a villager spotted forestry officials' mobile phones glowing in the darkness.
"They dug there and planted boundary stones," Velayutham said, pointing to the markers.
Repeated appeals to local authorities, the prime minister and president have brought no result, he said.
"This land has neither been freed nor handed back to us," he said. "If they release this farmland and we get it back from the Forest Department, I believe this will provide a great opportunity."
Land disputes have multiplied across the Eastern Province, where Tamils are a major ethnic group.
Examples include an army barracks encroaching on a school, while government departments responsible for archaeology, wildlife or forests claim farmland, temples and private property.

Officials designate land cultivated by Tamils as forest or wildlife reserves, "obstructing development or agricultural activities for them", said Sabarathinam Sivayoganathan, 57, president of the Eastern Province Civil Society Activists Union.
The scale of these occupations is unclear, with no public statistics and residents risking intimidation by asking questions, he said.
'Frustration'
Opposition MP Rasamanickam R. Shanakiyan says population figures point to a deliberate effort to change the region's demographics.
"In the Eastern Province, the Sinhala population has increased by 700% since independence in 1948," he said, compared with 200% nationally.
"This has happened through state-sponsored colonisation," he said, accusing the government of altering the ethnic balance of the north and east through land settlements.
President Anura Kumara Dissanayake's election in 2024 has brought little change, Shanakiyan said, despite campaign promises to the contrary.
He accused the government of failing to honour commitments in the lead up to the election that it would release land, protect minority rights and deliver wider political reforms.
"On these promises, nothing's been delivered," he said. "You feel a growing sense of frustration, maybe anger in the population."
Land ownership disputes continue to fuel tensions, resentment and accusations between Sinhalese and Tamils across eastern Sri Lanka, both online and on the ground.
The government says it has commissioned a report on changes to land records since the civil war and whether they should be corrected.
"We will never forcibly acquire people's land," Environment Minister Dhammika Patabendi told AFP in an email.
"Based on the recommendations of this report, we believe that these issues can be resolved promptly and fairly," he said.
But as torrential rain drums on the tarpaulin sheltering the angry farmers, Thiyagarajah remains unconvinced.
"For 1,010 days, alongside this road and under this tent, we have been taking part day and night. Justice has still not been granted to our people," he said.
"Today, our people live in constant fear that today or tomorrow our cattle will be destroyed."

c7ae2c231c8043ff: WASHINGTON: Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro will be granted entry into the United States, Washington said Tuesday, amid media reports that he has left Brazil for the country despite a court order banning his exit.
The son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro lost the presidential election Sunday to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and refused to concede defeat.
The US state department said Tuesday it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them entry into the United States, without confirming his travel plans.
The 45-year-old arrived in the United States Tuesday, CNN and the Washington Post reported, each citing an anonymous source. But where he landed remains unknown.

The right-wing senator on Monday said a Supreme Court justice had ordered him to hand over his passports. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.
A police source told AFP that the senator's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been cancelled, adding that "there is no formal record of Flavio Bolsonaro leaving the country."
But he has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP.
Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho expressed shock over reports that the defeated candidate had fled Brazil.
"We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," he told reporters Tuesday in Brasilia.
"I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," Marinho said.
"That was the only communication we had."
'Shameful'
Lula called fleeing the country a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful," he remarked in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration.
Bolsonaro said Monday that the ban on his exit from Brazil amounted to a scare tactic.
"I never had any intention of leaving the country," he said in a video posted on Instagram.
US president Donald Trump, a close ally of Jair Bolsonaro, on Monday said Brazil's elections were "rigged" following the defeat of Bolsonaro junior.
Flavio's brother Eduardo, a US-based former lawmaker, maintains close ties with the White House.
Last week, he told a US podcast that Flavio Bolsonaro should leave Brazil in the event of electoral defeat, given the active probes into his activities.
In his Monday statement, Lula's challenger also said he would lead the opposition to the leftist government.

Following Lula's victory with 51.8% of the vote, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting.
Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country.
In his father's footsteps
All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month.
He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.
Separately on Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered police to investigate alleged foreign funding of Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign and other interference from abroad such as social media "manipulation."
Lula's campaign complained about election interference by Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, claiming "algorithmic manipulation."
Meta denies taking any actions to favor one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.

c0647cc3ad278bdc: BERLIN, Oct 28 — German semiconductor maker Infineon said Tuesday it would invest €1.1 billion (RM4.99 billion) in a next-generation chip production unit in Austria to meet rising demand driven by the AI boom.

The group, based near Munich, said it intends to create the “world’s first high-volume manufacturing facility” for a specific kind of “next-generation” power semiconductor made using gallium nitride (GaN).
“Gallium nitride enables significant efficiency gains in numerous applications, such as AI data centres, energy infrastructure, e-mobility, robotics and consumer electronics,” the group said.
The new investment will expand the production capacity of Infineon’s Villach site in Austria by 2034, but the first chips are expected to be manufactured well before then, by the end of 2027.
Nearly 30 per cent of the investment is financed by European subsidies under the European Chips Act, which aims to strengthen the EU’s technological sovereignty.
The announcement gave Infineon a boost on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, with its share price up 2.3 per cent around noon.
Power chips, used in particular in vehicle engines and household appliances, are Infineon’s speciality.
They differ from the graphics processing units (GPUs) of US company Nvidia, which enable the development of AI models thanks to their high computing power.
But for some time now, Infineon has been reducing its dependence on the crisis-hit automotive industry to move into supplying the AI sector, notably by equipping data centres.
In July, Infineon made the largest investment in its history with the inauguration of a new chip factory in the eastern German city of Dresden worth €5 billion. — AFP
331feda3c40d3cbf: SINGAPORE: The pounding of running shoes echoes through a Singapore shopping mall as fitness enthusiasts desperate to exercise take refuge from choking haze.
Smoke from wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia has sent air quality in the city-state plummeting to its worst levels in more than a decade in recent weeks, cancelling outdoor activities.
Those seeking exercise, including runners training for international events, have found an unconventional alternative: air-conditioned shopping malls.
On Sunday more than 80 runners turned the corridors of Marina Square shopping centre into makeshift running tracks, clocking laps past storefronts on two floors before shops opened for business.
There are strict rules.
"No sprinting, no overtaking, no shouting or yelling," Eugene Beh, 52, founder of Singapore Runners Club, told about 60 members before their run.
Spitting and wiping sweat on the floor are also banned.
Beh said they had to cancel several runs outdoors because of the haze, blown in by the wind from forest and peatland fires in Borneo and Sumatra.
'Very mental'
Angeline Zeng, 57, who works in banking, completed 10 loops at the mall, or about 10km.
With a half-marathon in Taipei in less than a week and a full marathon in December, Zeng needs to clock as much mileage as she can.
Since treadmills at her neighbourhood gym are often full, she and her fellow runners were excited when they heard about the mall runs.
"We were like, wow, we didn't expect that at all," she told AFP.
"I love it because the aircon makes you feel like you're running overseas where there's cold temperatures, so it's really great," Zeng added.
But she said that circling inside the mall becomes "boring" after a while.
"Maybe for shorter runs this is okay but if you need to do long runs, maybe not so suitable," she said.
Singapore Runners Club member Doris Tan, 42, said she thought running indoors would be a bit suffocating.
"I didn't expect it to be so cool... but if you have to ask me, I still prefer outdoors," she told AFP.
Paul Wong, a 54-year-old retiree from a club called X-Run, completed 21 loops inside the mall, or about 21 km.

With just over a month until the Singapore International Marathon - which many other fellow runners are also training for - Wong would have to run up to 80km per week, but the haze has forced him indoors.
"For the last two weeks I've been running close to 100km on the treadmill. The longest I've run is 28km for two and a half hours, it's very mental," Wong said.
"The mall run is definitely better because the treadmill feels like a hamster run. You just keep repeating the routine."
Eddie Chan, lead coach for X-Run, said they had to present a carefully laid-out plan to get approval from the mall for the runs.
They had to consider factors like walkway width, tight corners and holding the run early in the morning before the shops open.
Just the start?
"The biggest challenge for outdoor training is the weather. Humidity is very high, plus the haze now, the impact is doubled and tripled, so it's very hard to manage," Chan told AFP.
"By converting to indoors, you definitely reduce all the impact from the outdoor experience and continue running."
The air quality improved this week but on Wednesday Singapore remained one of the 20 most polluted major cities in the world, according to Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir.
The two running clubs are likely to extend the mall runs if poor air quality persists, and plan to ask more malls to open their doors to them.
"I believe there will be opportunities. This is something new in the sports scene," Beh said.
"Hopefully, with the permission of building management, this can spread out to other sports groups."
781df1c888a1032b: SYDNEY: Australian police have charged a man with falsely claiming he was injured in a mass shooting at Sydney's Bondi Beach in an attempt to gain financial compensation.
A father-and-son duo allegedly carried out the gun attack on a Jewish festival at the beach in December last year, killing 15 people and wounding dozens.

Police said they arrested the man on Tuesday and charged him with publishing false and misleading material to obtain advantage.
He was given conditional bail, and is scheduled to appear in western Sydney's Parramatta Local Court on Nov 18.
One of the Bondi Beach gunmen, Sajid Akram, 50, was shot and killed by police during the Dec 14 attack. An Indian national, he entered Australia on a visa in 1998.
His son Naveed, an Australian-born citizen, remains in custody facing a total of 78 charges including terrorism and 15 murders.
A Sydney court on Wednesday set Naveed Akram's committal hearing for Feb 24 next year, when he is set to appear by audio-video link from prison.
He has yet to enter a plea.

42bbb783785ff1ab: PETALING JAYA: Police have frozen or seized assets worth more than RM409 million in an ongoing investigation into allegations of a "corporate mafia" involving the abuse of enforcement powers to pressure businessmen into selling company shares at below-market prices.

"No Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) officers were involved or identified as individuals required to assist with the investigation," he said.
