43da1b702e3e00a8: MUMBAI: India's Jio Platforms makes its stock market debut on Wednesday after a record-breaking IPO, capping billionaire owner Mukesh Ambani's years-long drive to diversify his conglomerate beyond oil refining.

Jio Platforms, which houses the country's biggest wireless operator and is the digital services arm of Ambani's Reliance Industries, raised about US$3.2 billion at 1,119 rupees (US$11.76) per share in India's biggest-ever initial public offering.
The listing, one of the year's most anticipated, attracted robust demand last week, with investors applying for more than 22 times the shares on offer.

In the run-up to its Mumbai debut, grey market platforms showed a premium of around 22% for Jio shares, although experts caution that such unofficial indicators can be unreliable predictors of early trading.
Nevertheless, most analysts expect decent listing gains despite a weak year for Indian equities.

Jio has a "proven execution record" and will see its cash generation "strengthening as the 5G investment cycle winds down", analysts at financial services firm Emkay Global said in a note, calling the company "the digital engine of India".
Launched a decade ago, Jio's wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts, rapidly winning customers from rivals Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.
With over 530 million subscribers, the firm currently makes most of its money from telecoms, but has expanded in recent years into digital services and artificial intelligence.
Experts say Jio is key to Reliance's strategy to move beyond oil and underpins its future technology ambitions.

Local media have reported how it is considering a low Earth orbit satellite constellation to provide internet services from space -- a venture that would see it compete with Musk's Starlink, which has been trying for years to launch in India.
Musk accused unnamed Indian "oligarchs" this month of preventing Starlink's rollout in the country, and referred to the Reliance chairman as "Prime Minister Ambani" and the "real boss of India".
Reliance responded by noting that it had never "feared competition" and welcomed offerings from rivals in satellite communications, including Starlink.
0c5ad1c0294ef26e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Nestle (Malaysia) Bhd shares emerged as top gainer in early trade today following a stronger performance in the third quarter ended September 30, 2026 (3Q 2026).
Its net profit rose to RM197.51 million in 3Q 2026, compared with RM114.04 million in the same quarter a year ago, supported by higher sales.

Revenue also advanced 5.3 per cent to RM1.86 billion during the quarter from RM1.76 billion previously, driven by stronger domestic demand across key product categories, supported by continued innovation and effective commercial execution, the company said in a Bursa Malaysia filing yesterday.

Meanwhile, RHB Investment Bank Bhd said Nestle Malaysia was well on track for another year of sustained resurgence, supported by accommodative government fiscal policies, improved consumer sentiment towards its brands, and disciplined cost controls to protect profit margins.

“We maintain our positive stance on Nestle Malaysia, premised on the appeal of its defensive earnings profile. The company is well positioned to benefit from the government’s fiscal support approach whilst gross profit margin tailwinds could sustain at least in the immediate term.
“Therefore, we maintained a ‘buy’ call on Nestle Malaysia with a new target price of RM130 per share,” it said in a note today.
At 10.08am, the company’s shares rose RM4.60 to RM98.88 with a total of 30,800 shares traded. — Bernama
dbb3879ba196e27d: SINGAPORE: Asia stocks rallied on Wednesday after a resurgence in AI enthusiasm ahead of earnings from industry bellwethers later in the US day, while the dollar was perky ahead of a Federal Reserve policy decision.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix reporting a more than seven-fold rise in quarterly operating profit added to the buoyant mood.

The AI rally faces its next test when technology giants Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings after market close, with investors looking for evidence of returns that would justify the hefty price of AI build-out.

"While we're expecting strong results across the board, the focus is less about the actual earnings results than about whether the capex spending for AI growth will translate into sustainable revenue growth for these companies, which remains a big question mark," said SWBC chief investment officer Chris Brigati.

"The period of a rising market lifting all stocks has started to shift. Future expectations are more focused upon execution risk and how much future success is already embedded in the current stock price."
Ahead of US earnings, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 0.85% in early Asia trade, with Japan's Nikkei adding 1.2% and South Korea's KOSPI jumping more than 3%.
Shares of SK Hynix rose 3% shortly after open, before paring gains to last trade 1.75% higher.

A series of AI-related funding announcements from Meta, SpaceX and Broadcom this week has breathed new life into the AI trade, with sentiment further boosted by Anthropic's initial public offering filing.
US futures were little changed, while EUROSTOXX 50 futures edged 0.03% lower.
What will the Fed do?
Earnings aside, investors are watching for the Fed's policy decision later on Wednesday, where a steady outcome is widely expected.
Market focus, however, will be on what policymakers say regarding the outlook for interest rates, with inflation concern still front and centre as war in the Middle East drags on.
Analysts at JPMorgan said in a client note they anticipate at least two hawkish dissents.
"Market participants will likely focus on how Chair (Kevin) Warsh couches the decision, and we think deferring on an explanation will be viewed as dovish in nature," they said.
Ahead of the decision, the dollar index held near a two-week high against six major currencies at 102.37.
Meanwhile, the kiwi tumbled more than 1% after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand confounded market expectations by leaving its policy interest rate unchanged.

The Australian dollar rose 0.25% to US$0.7043 following data which showed consumer prices rose sharply in the third quarter of the year as fuel costs jumped, while core inflation stayed uncomfortably hot.
In Israel, the shekel weakened after exit polls showed the country's wartime election appeared deadlocked.
In oil markets, Brent crude futures were up 0.47% at US$114.42 a barrel and US crude added 0.55% to US$100.45.

An agreement to end the US-Israeli war with Iran remains elusive. Iranian security council chief Mohsen Rezaei met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Tuesday, a day after talks with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.
580318bb96df7b4c: SAN FRANCISCO: No startup has ever grown so fast. In five years, Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion, and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut.
But it faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spells out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, published Monday.
The first is commoditisation: "The degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow," the company warns.

The San Francisco-based firm also says "substantially all of our revenue" comes from its AI tools. Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft's or SpaceX's.
Investors have already grown nervous. In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion.
But quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145% in the second quarter to 45% in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.5 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are close behind closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners' paid services.
The performance of open models trails by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures "could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints."
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80 percent of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text at the same level of performance, has dropped 97%, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20% in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13% in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
Even a 90% price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace, said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
'Triple whammy'
Anthropic's costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancellable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic's shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a "triple whammy" from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materializes.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing "an unprecedented test of investor gullibility."
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centers, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing "ill-advised" this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival.
1bea0bf7e2205649: LONDON: Britain's finance minister John Healey will unveil his first budget Wednesday, as he juggles commitments to defence spending and easing household bills with little financial room to manoeuvre.

It could prove to be a tall order for prime minister Andy Burnham's new administration as rising inflation and borrowing costs - largely a consequence of the US-Iran war - increase the government's debt pile and heap pressure on businesses and individuals.
"We can't stop these shocks that hit Britain, but we can make Britain more resilient when they do," Healey said in a statement released on the eve of the Labour government's budget.
"This budget is about getting through this difficult moment," he said, adding that it would provide "breathing space" for households and "targeted support" for businesses.

Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, said Monday the latest annual tax and spending plans will set out how the government intends to finance the defence investment programme laid out by his predecessor.
Healey is expected to delay until next year details of how Britain will meet Nato's target of defence spending reaching 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
Healey resigned as defence minister under Starmer, accusing the Treasury of insufficient military funding.
Labour had ruled out rises to income and capital gains tax, raising the prospect of spending cuts to balance the books, according to analysts.
'Small-scale' budget

Healey, whose official title is chancellor of the exchequer, has also pledged to abide by the rules laid out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, which state that day-to-day spending must balance with government tax receipts.
The chancellor is expected to use a windfall tax on banks to fund a package of spending measures to help households manage rising energy bills.
"This budget will largely be a stopgap that will tide the government over before a more significant policy overhaul in 2027," said Alexander Harvey, UK economist at Oxford Economics.
"The measures will be fairly small-scale ones to ease the cost of living, as well as other relatively low-cost policies," he added.
Some relatively low-cost relief measures have already been announced, including cuts to tariffs on more than 100 imported goods and an expansion of the parental pay regime.
Further measures could include an extension of a freeze on fuel duty, more targeted help for the poorest households and an increase in the minimum wage, according to reports.
Surging diesel costs at the pump helped push Britain's annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September, the highest rate for nearly a year.
The government last week approved drilling in a North Sea gas field, claiming the move was aimed at boosting energy security rather than cutting bills.
The budget will also include measures to reduce "pointless paperwork" to lower costs for businesses, according to Healey.
A package of investment in artificial intelligence safety was announced by the Treasury over the weekend, amid growing global concerns over the cyber and biological risks posed by AI.
Surging borrowing costs
The government's fiscal headroom of £23.6 billion (US$31.4 billion) is expected to be slashed in an update given alongside the budget, as higher borrowing costs hike the state's debt repayments.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, an independent financial watchdog, will on Wednesday also publish its latest UK growth and inflation forecasts.
Government bond yields around the world have struck multi-decade highs in recent weeks as wider inflation climbs largely because of energy prices soaring on wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Rising inflation has cemented expectations that the Bank of England will hike its benchmark interest rate next month, further pressuring Britons holding loans, including mortgages.
a254d1078b639f92: Indian tech services giant Infosys has mixed news about AI.
In its most recent quarterly results late last week, the company revealed that it’s racked up 29 percent sequential growth in AI revenue, which now delivers 10.5 percent of Infosys’ incoming cash.
Those are far nicer numbers than the 1.5 percent year-on-year revenue growth Infosys reported for its second quarter.

“Growth was below our expectations. Volume was softer, and price increases were lower than anticipated amid high competitive intensity,” chief financial officer Jayesh Sanghrajka told investors. One reason for lower price increases was that customers expect Infosys to charge less when it uses AI, and those cost savings are now “baked in” to its multi-year deals.
CEO and managing director Salil Parekh also pointed to AI as one reason the cost of services is falling.

“I think what we see today is there is definitely some of our peers who are putting, I would say, more intense effort into the pricing pressure,” he said, “but it is also across the board because of the environment and also the discussion on AI productivity. If you are talking with clients today on large programs, it is a three or five-year outlook.”
That leaves Infosys dependent on new work from AI to boost revenue growth, while AI also makes it hard to keep growing revenue from existing customers.

Infosys won’t go low to win deals and intends to hold its margins at around 21 percent, Sanghrajka said. He sought to prove that point by citing “a large deal that we walked out of, or we did not pursue because it did not meet our return expectations.”
To help preserve margins, the company is conducting “Project Maximus” to find efficiencies within its own operations. AI-powered tools to win more sales are also in the mix.

The company sees difficult months ahead. Sanghrajka said the retail and high-tech industries have slowed their services spending and acknowledged that the second half of Infosys’s financial year is usually its slow period.

The company tried to convince investors that they have little to worry about, pointing to $8.8 billion of new deals won in the first half of its financial year – 68 percent of which were net new customers – as a sign that Infosys’ fundamentals are sound.

But the company also offered less optimistic guidance about its future. In its Q1 results, Infosys predicted full-year revenue growth of 1.5 to 3.0 percent. In Q2, it revised that prediction to 1.0 to 2.0 percent.

Infosys’s share price didn’t dive after that news but is already down over 25 percent in the last twelve months. And Bloomberg reports that investment analysts have downgraded the company, suggesting they feel its prospects are poor. ®

230f68927ddac655: NEW YORK, Oct 28 — Boeing shares plunged Tuesday as the company’s cautious production growth timeframe surprised Wall Street, deepening questions about how fast recent plane certification and defense procurement wins will translate to the bottom line.
The aviation giant ended the day down 10.7 per cent, the worst performer in the Dow index, as investors reacted poorly to forecasts from Boeing leaders on a conference call.
Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg said the company does not expect 737 MAX output to reach 52 per month until the second half of 2027 as it must first “stabilize” output at 47 per month.
Raising 737 MAX output has been viewed by investors as central to revenue and profit growth. But Ortberg, who joined Boeing in the aftermath of safety disasters, defended the approach.

“We’re making progress, but we still have more work to do, and I’m expecting it’ll take us into next year to get fully stable at this rate,” Ortberg said of the 47 planes per month, citing the need for greater predictability in wing production and with the production of fuselages at its Kansas operation.
“It’s more important that we do this ramp right than what particular month we achieve a rate break,” Ortberg said.
Ortberg also put a timeframe on when the company will achieve US$10 billion (RM40.8 billion) in annual free cash flow, saying it will reach the key target of financial health in 2029.
After Ortberg gave this timeframe, shares fell further, suggesting analysts had expected a quicker pace.
“Everybody wants us to go faster. I get that, but we’re going to stay disciplined as we ramp up here,” Ortberg said.

Ortberg joined Boeing as CEO in August 2024 as the company struggled to move past a pair of deadly 737 MAX crashes and a near-catastrophic 737 MAX flight in January 2024 in which a window blew out mid-flight.
The company at the time faced criticism that the problems stemmed from a culture that chased quick payoffs while shortchanging safety.

Boeing is making “slow but steady” progress, aviation expert Richard Aboulafia of AeroDynamic Advisory said in an email to AFP. “But the supply chain remains a major concern and one that’s only partly in Boeing’s control.”
Smaller loss

Ortberg’s comments came as Boeing reported a third-quarter loss of US$116 million, compared with a loss of US$5.3 billion in the year-ago period mostly from delays to certification of the 777X, the latest generation in Boeing’s long-range, wide-body commercial jet family.
The results translated into a larger earnings-per-share loss than analysts expected, but shares did not move significantly after the earnings press release was published.

Ortberg cited the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification of the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10 as well as a “transformational” Pentagon award for the US Navy’s next-generation fighter jets as evidence of momentum.
Revenues rose four per cent to US$24.2 billion behind increased deliveries in its defense, space and security business and higher sales in Boeing Global Services.
Revenues for commercial aircraft dipped from the year-ago period, with it delivering 161 aircraft in the quarter, just one more than in the 2025 period.
Boeing executives expressed confidence the much-delayed 777X would be certified in 2027, projecting deliveries of between 10 and 15 next year of that aircraft.
“We’re providing this with confidence that the team’s ready to go execute,” Ortberg said of the latest targets.
Ortberg expects free cash flow to gradually grow from about US$2 billion in 2026 to US$6 billion in 2028 to US$10 billion in 2029 and higher levels after that.

“As I mentioned, over the last two years, we’ve made exceptional progress restoring trust, retiring risk, and transforming our culture and rebuilding the foundation of safety and quality that will help ensure durable success,” he said.
“We have also been deliberate about not getting ahead of ourselves, given the range of outcomes tied to the production ramp, certification timing, and other critical program execution,” he said.

“But we appreciate that it’s been difficult for share owners to assess how our progress will translate into financial performance. We’re now at a point where the range of outcomes is narrowing.” — AFP
3e0e11ce56af055e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Bursa Malaysia opened higher on Wednesday as market sentiment improved, tracking overnight gains on Wall Street following fresh artificial intelligence (AI)-related funding announcements.
At 9.10am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 3.39 points, or 0.21 per cent, to 1,615.24 from Tuesday’s close of 1,611.85.
The benchmark index opened 2.64 points higher at 1,614.49.
Across the broader market, gainers outpaced losers 251 to 94, while 297 counters were unchanged, 2,225 untraded, and 104 suspended.
Turnover stood at 218.30 million units worth RM87.52 million.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said overnight Wall Street ended higher as investors turned their attention to upcoming corporate earnings reports, particularly those from the technology sector.
“Back home, the FBM KLCI closed higher yesterday above the 1,610 level on bargain hunting, supported mainly by local funds.
“Buying interest was evident in utility counters, which came under heavy selling pressure the previous day. For today, we expect the index to hover within the 1,605-1,615 range,” he told Bernama.

Among the heavyweight stocks, Maybank rose one sen to RM10.00, while CIMB added two sen to RM7.13. Public Bank, Tenaga Nasional and IHH Healthcare were all flat at RM4.75, RM13.30 and RM7.84, respectively.

In active trade, Zetrix AI and MQ Technology inched up half a sen each to nine sen and six sen, respectively. V.S Industry, MYMBN and Dagang Nexchange added one sen each to 35.5 sen, 17.5 sen and 45 sen, respectively.

Nestle led the top gainers, adding RM2.38 to RM96.66, while Malaysian Pacific Industries added 30 sen to RM41.60. Far East Holdings rose 25 sen to RM4.20, while MI Technovation and Hong Leong Bank went up 16 sen each to RM6.91 and RM21.36, respectively.

Among the top losers, United Plantations lost 38 sen to RM29.32, Westports Holdings declined 16 sen to RM6.92, Farm Fresh decreased seven sen to RM1.81, SAM Engineering & Equipment slid six sen to RM4.25 and Hengyuan Refining Company shed five sen to RM4.06.

On the index board, the FBM Emas Index increased 23.53 points to 12,062.82, the FBM Top 100 Index rose 21.02 points to 11,855.55, the FBM Mid 70 Index gained 14.68 points to 17,384.80, the FBM Emas Shariah Index was 20.98 points higher at 12,070.71 and the FBM ACE Index went up 27.12 points to 5,445.75.

Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index edged up 0.30 of a point to 177.21, the Energy Index increased 6.30 points to 852.04, the Financial Services Index jumped 31.79 points to 18,632.82 and the Plantation Index improved 6.32 points to 8,660.58. — Bernama
f2c2b0ff3ea7b210: NEW YORK, Oct 28 — Wall Street stocks rose for a second straight session Tuesday behind renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence-linked shares as markets awaited a Federal Reserve decision and earnings from big AI players.

Major US indices advanced, led by the tech-rich Nasdaq, which capitalised on AI enthusiasm following Anthropic’s IPO filing while also greeting an announcement from Broadcom about a major new financing deal for AI investment.

“The buy-the-dip trade is taking place,” said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O’Hare. “You have the market being led by the AI stocks and particularly the semiconductors and those larger hyperscaler names.”
In a share-launch filing Monday, Anthropic, the mother company for Claude AI, reported first-half revenue surged about 1,300 per cent year-on-year, but also flagged heavy capital spending ahead.
Investors are awaiting earnings this week from Magnificent Seven members Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon as well as SK hynix and Samsung.

“The fact that this five year-old company could soon launch a record-breaking IPO helped boost investor confidence, following a decidedly rocky period across AI-adjacent corporations of late,” said David Morrison, an analyst at Trade Nation.
Tech shares were under pressure much of last week on worries that massive AI investments might not pay off and that heavily indebted companies face difficulty due to higher interest rates.

But markets being more generous this week. Broadcom climbed four per cent after announcing jointly with Citi, Blackstone and Morgan Stanley a US$63 billion (RM257 billion) financing structure to build new capacity for Anthropic.
The Nasdaq piled on more than one per cent, while the Dow edged higher, though pressured in part by a 10.7 per cent drop in Boeing shares after the aviation giant reported results.
In London, the benchmark FTSE 100 index was dragged down by HSBC, whose share price fell 5.4 per cent after its bumper profits undershot market expectations.
Mercedes-Benz shed 3.8 per cent in Frankfurt after the German carmaker cut its full-year outlook, underperforming the DAX index which slightly rose overall in afternoon trading. Paris also rose.
Earlier, equities rose in Japan and Korea, also boosted by Anthropic’s IPO filing.
Seoul’s stock market briefly jumped more than four per cent Tuesday thanks to strong gains in chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung.
Tokyo added 1.8 per cent on spikes in Tokyo Electron, Advantest and SoftBank.

“Sentiment towards technology has improved as investors assess Anthropic’s IPO filing at the start of a week packed with corporate earnings and the Federal Reserve’s rate decision,” said Fiona Cincotta at FOREX.com.

IG analyst Chris Beauchamp said “there remains hope that this is a more durable rally than those we saw last week, with the caveat that there is still an abundance of macro risk to navigate this week.”
The Fed is expected to keep interest rates on hold in a decision Wednesday, though CME Group’s FedWatch tool says there is a 78 per cent chance of a hike when it meets in December as inflation rises.
Those expectations have boosted the dollar.
The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan are also expected to hold tight in announcements on Thursday and Friday.
Oil prices fell amid renewed diplomatic efforts to resolve the Middle East conflict and as Israelis went to the polls in parliamentary elections. — AFP

ecd8875168689450: SAN FRANCISCO: OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips, The Information reported on Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter, as technology companies ramp up spending on data centres and semiconductors to meet surging demand for AI computing.
The planned purchase would deepen ties between OpenAI and Alphabet's Google, which compete in AI products and search. The report did not disclose financial terms or other details.
Google did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours, while OpenAI declined to comment.
OpenAI is one of the largest buyers of Nvidia's graphics processing units, or GPUs, which the ChatGPT maker uses to train AI models and run inference computing.
Reuters reported in June 2025 that OpenAI had begun renting Google's AI chips.

Google's Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, have gained traction as an alternative to Nvidia's market-leading AI chips as companies seek cheaper options and chips suited to running AI models. Google began selling TPUs directly to some customers this year.
Alphabet will report its quarterly results later on Wednesday, with investors looking for signs that its heavy investment in AI is continuing to drive growth in its cloud business.
b5347f83840f22b6: SEOUL, Oct 28 — South Korean chip giant SK hynix said Wednesday its third-quarter operating profit soared 632 per cent on-year, largely driven by the artificial intelligence industry’s explosive demand for its advanced memory chips.
Operating profit for the July-September period was 83.33 trillion won (RM256.6 billion), the company said.
The firm’s July-September net profit jumped 215.7 per cent from last year to 39.77 trillion won, while sales reached 104.61 trillion won.
The memory chip giant said it had posted record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters since the second quarter of last year.
But the earnings fell behind market expectations. The average estimate of net profit by analysts stood at 59.67 trillion won, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency, citing its own data firm.

“SK hynix analysed that a virtuous cycle has taken hold in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue generation in areas such as software development, customer service, and search lead to greater AI adoption,” the chipmaker said in a statement.
SK hynix is a specialist supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to US industry behemoth Nvidia, and a pillar of South Korea’s tech-led economy.
The global race to build AI data centres has transformed the company’s fortunes, despite concerns that the sector may be overvalued.

In high demand are key chips known as DRAM and storage components called NAND, which are found in everyday gadgets but are also needed to help process the vast amounts of data crunched by generative AI.

Analysts say soaring DRAM prices amid a global shortage and stronger sales of high-margin high-bandwidth memory (HBM) have driven earnings, while the AI boom has also lifted prices and shipments of conventional NAND chips.
Not yet peaked

Long-term agreements established with major customers, including Nvidia, signal “another phase of price increase across both conventional DRAM, NAND and HBM”, MS Hwang, an analyst at market research firm Counterpoint, told AFP.
“This indicates that quarterly earnings have not yet reached their peak and that the upward trajectory will likely sustain at least through 2027.”
But the company’s shares have been under pressure since June, as investors largely shrugged off record quarterly earnings that had already been priced in.
Going into 2027, “weaker AI spending, increased competition, and the company’s own capacity expansion are all factors that dictate price volatility,” analyst Hwang said.
“The single most severe threat would be a scenario reminiscent of 2018, where cloud service providers simultaneously pull back on their order volumes.”
Record profits from booming AI memory demand have fuelled investor calls for the company to return more cash through dividends or buybacks.
Those calls have grown since its shares retreated from record highs in June amid concerns over the outlook for US tech firms’ AI spending.
SK hynix announced an additional plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders on Wednesday, following the completion of a 40 trillion-won shareholder return programme.

“The company’s stock has fallen nearly 60 per cent from its peak (in June), and I think that is the main reason the company needs to focus on winning back shareholders”, Kim Dae-jong, a professor of business administration at Sejong University, told AFP.
“Stock prices tend to anticipate future conditions rather than simply reflect current earnings,” he said.

“The concern is that the extraordinary level of earnings the company is generating today may not be sustainable one or two years from now, and I believe that concern is already being reflected in the share price.” — AFP
6f20fa3677e84710: From Cheli Tamilselvam Nadarajah
A school should be a place where children feel safe, friendships flourish, differences are respected, and every child knows that someone cares.
It should be a place where teachers inspire, parents trust, and children grow not only in knowledge but also in character.
Yet we read about tragic incidents of violence, bullying and the loss of young lives in our schools.
Could these tragedies have been prevented? Were there red flags? Did these children have someone to turn to?
Time to act
As an educator, I believe that a school’s greatest achievement is not simply excellent examination results, but the kind of human beings it nurtures.
What does academic excellence mean if a child is afraid to attend school, humiliated by classmates, or feels invisible within its walls?

I have had parents standing before me with tears in their eyes, asking for just one thing: that their children grow up to be good people. Their plea has stayed with me. Every child deserves an excellent education in a safe, caring and supportive environment.
Bullying is not merely a disciplinary issue that children will eventually outgrow. It can damage confidence, emotional wellbeing and a child’s sense of belonging.
While those who bully others must be held accountable, punishment alone may not change the attitudes and beliefs behind their behaviour.
We cannot condemn our children for displaying behaviours that we, as adults, have modelled, tolerated or failed to challenge.
We must protect victims, support affected children, address harmful behaviour and help every child learn responsibility, empathy and respect.
This requires more than occasional motivational talks or campaigns launched after a tragedy. It requires a sustained transformation of our school culture.
A lesson from SMK Bandar Kuching No 1

In 2006, while serving at SMK Bandar Kuching No 1 in Sarawak, I introduced the Attitude Breakthrough Challenge (ABC) to demonstrate that positive attitudes can be developed, and character strengthened through consistent practice and shared responsibility.
The initiative went beyond punishing misconduct.
It sought to empower teachers, engage parents and encourage students to take ownership of their behaviour. Students were encouraged to support one another in making better choices.
The aim was not to shame children or make them police their peers, but to build a community where positive behaviour was valued and everyone had a part to play.

Its key elements included peer accountability, teacher empowerment and parental engagement, supported by a structured system of merit and demerit codes, focusing more on the recognition of positive behaviour, and graduated responses to misconduct.

Student suspension cases recorded by the education ministry (MoE) fell from 136 in 2005 to fewer than 40 in 2006, followed by 16 in 2007, fewer than 10 in 2008, eight in 2009, six in 2010 and three in 2011.
For me, the greatest lesson was this: Negative behaviour need not be accepted as inevitable.
When teachers are empowered, parents are involved, students are accountable and positive behaviour is recognised, meaningful change becomes possible.
Making positive attitudes a way of life
The ABC, now rebranded as Positive Attitude Builds Character (PABC), must be more than a short-term programme or a slogan on a school wall; it must become a way of life.
Children need opportunities to practise positive values, supported by adults who model them and systems that reinforce them consistently.

While PABC is not a magic solution to every school safety challenge, its principles and practical experiences offer valuable lessons for a comprehensive approach to prevention, accountability, character development and student wellbeing.

We must distinguish between holding children accountable and labelling them as failures. Children who make mistakes need appropriate consequences, guidance and opportunities to change, while victims must be protected and serious misconduct addressed promptly.

A positive school culture does not happen by accident. It requires committed leadership, empowered teachers, engaged parents, responsible students and effective systems to identify problems early, monitor concerns and ensure timely follow-up.
A safe school is not one where no complaints are made. It is one where children feel safe enough to speak up and trust that adults will act.
I appeal to the MoE, school heads, parents and communities to make safe, happy and inclusive schools a national priority.
When a child feels safe, valued and happy at school, learning becomes more meaningful, relationships flourish, and every child has a greater opportunity to thrive.

Let us make the main thing the main thing: the wellbeing, character and future of our children. Amid the many demands, distractions and competing priorities that bombard us daily, we must never lose sight of what matters most.
Every child must know that someone cares
After more than four decades in education, I remain passionate about the potential of every child.

I believe in the teacher who encourages a struggling student, the school head who refuses to ignore a problem, the parent who sacrifices for a child’s future, and the child who can grow into a responsible and caring person when given the right guidance and support.

Children should not have to remember school as a place where they were afraid. They must remember it as a place where they discovered their abilities, built friendships, learnt to respect others and found adults who believed in them.
Teachers should not feel that they must fight these battles alone. They deserve to feel empowered, supported and valued.
We may not be able to prevent every difficulty a child faces in life, but we can do far more to ensure that school is never a place where a child has to live in fear.
Our children deserve better. They deserve schools that are safe, happy, caring and inclusive. The time to act is now.
Cheli Tamilselvam Nadarajah is a fomer school principal and an FMT reader.

a3c1ecdc3562be0b: Sultan Selangor yang menyambut jubli perak pemerintahannya tahun ini ada mesej tajam kepada golongan pembakar sentimen perkauman yang melihat diri sendiri sebagai wira sesuatu bangsa .
Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah dengan lantang menegur golongan itu - hentikan eksploitasi bangsa dan agama untuk mendapat keuntungan politik dan jangan mengheret istana ke dalam pertikaian mereka.

Titah baginda datang ketika arena politik Malaysia dicengkam permainan sentimen ras dan agama dimana hak Melayu, identiti Islam dan kedudukan masyarakat bukan Melayu berulang kali diketengahkan, secara negatif.

Lihat sahaja PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan yang diadakan tahun ini. Sentimen perkauman ditiup dan dibakar. Ferociously – to a level never seen before. Selain dua PRN itu, hampir semua perkara dijadikan isu bangsa dan agama di merata tempat. Politik perkauman (atau kata sesetengah orang politik identiti) dimainkan sewenang-wenangnya.

Daripada kempen pilihan raya, dibawa ke perdebatan di Parlimen, menembusi platform media sosial naratif politik berkisar tentang siapa yang konon akan kerugian, kehilangan hak, diancam dan terancam serta siapa yang benar-benar wira mempertahankan bangsa dan agama tertentu.
Retorik politikus mencetuskan naratif perkauman melampau dalam kalangan warganet yang merupakan ‘rakyat biasa’ dan pastinya golongan yang digelar atau mahu dianggap ‘laskar siber’.
Kata kolumnis politik, Lim Hong Siang, negara berada dalam situasi kebangkitan kumpulan sayap kanan ekstrem yang mengancam realiti kepelbagaian dan kebebasan.

Pada 15 Okt lalu, Ahli Parlimen Puncak Borneo Willie Mongin berkongsi maklumat di Dewan Rakyat seorang guru baru-baru ini memberitahunya, ada dalam kalangan anak sekolah yang tidak mahu duduk sebelah rakan sekelas bukan sebangsa dan seagama dengan mereka.

Daripada mana atau daripada siapa anak-anak ‘belajar’ tabiat tidak baik begitu? Kemungkinan besar daripada ibu bapa yang termakan kata-kata berbaur perkauman sang politikus dan dakyah negatif dimainkan di media sosial.

Mongin tidak beritahu di mana sekolah perkara itu berlaku. Bagi saya jika ia berlaku di Borneo yang terkenal dengan muhibah dan toleransi antara kaumnya, saya tidak terkejut jika itu juga ada berlaku di Semenanjung.
Semua ini mengancam perpaduan rakyat – merenggang hubungan antara kaum. Ramai pandai menyakiti dan ramai pula yang disakiti.
Dengan PRN Melaka pula akan diadakan tidak lama lagi pasti atau hampir pasti taktik eksploitasi ras dan agama akan diulangi politikus sebagai jalan pintas untuk mendapat kemenangan di peti undi.
Sememangnya memperalatkan isu bangsa dan agama mudah menarik perhatian dan sekali gus mendapat sokongan.

Lantas teguran Sultan Sharafuddin tepat pada masanya. Baginda tidak menamakan sesiapa. Namun, kita tahu siapa yang dimaksudkan. Kita tahu siapa penggemar permainan politik perkauman. No prizes for guessing.
The Sultan’s patience is wearing thin. “Seperti rakyat, beta juga bosan,” titah Sultan Sharafuddin yang dilapor Malaysiakini, Isnin lalu.

Baginda menyeru semua ahli politik Selangor memberi fokus terhadap serving the people, perkhidmatan baik untuk rakyat, menjana pertumbuhan ekonomi dan memastikan perpaduan yang terjalin dalam kalangan rakyat terus dipupuk dan dijaga .

Demi memastikan Selangor maintains it’s leading position in the country. Titah baginda kekuatan Selangor ialah pada rakyatnya. “Kita dianugerah masyarakat berbilang bangsa, kebudayaan dan agama yang generasi ke generasi telah hidup dan bekerja bersama dalam harmoni mencapai kemakmuran.”

Titah baginda, sememangnya boleh dirujuk atau diguna pakai untuk seluruh Malaysia bukan sahaja Selangor. Dan saranan Sultan Sharafuddin kepada ahli politik memang boleh dituju kepada semua ahli politik di semua negeri. Politikus pemain politik perkauman are everywhere in the country.

Sebenarnya, memang raja Melayu lain juga seperti Sultan Sharufuddin mahu permainan politik perkauman dinyahkan. Kita pernah dengar saranan, teguran serta nasihat mereka. Cuma politikus degil tetap degil. Yang gemar main sentimen ras untuk kemenangan pilihan raya meneruskan kegemaran mereka. Tanpa hirau nasihat raja tanpa menghiraukan kesejahteraan rakyat dan negeri masing-masing dan juga negara.

Sehingga kini, seperti Sultan Selangor, raja-raja tidak atau belum namakan sesiapa. Namun, mungkin akan tiba masa Sultan Selangor dan raja-raja lain akan menamakan politikus yang terus-menerus jadikan bangsa dan agama isu untuk dapat manfaat peti undi konon atas nama bangsa dan agama.
Mungkin akan tiba masa raja-raja mendedahkan identiti mereka kepada rakyat meskipun rakyat tahu siapa mereka .

Ini tidak mustahil berlaku, kerana bak titah Sultan Sharafuddin yang dinyatakan tadi baginda sudah bosan dengan gelagat politikus meniup sentimen perkauman. Saya yakin the other rulers are equally fed up. Their patience are also wearing thin.

394a6f85314f6ac9: From Boo Jia Cher
Recently, a friend shared a photo on social media celebrating the return of blue skies and air quality readings returning to "good" after weeks of haze.
At first glance, the photo felt uplifting. The sky was clear and cloudless.
But what caught my attention was what sat directly beneath it: a vast expanse of low-density suburbia sliced apart by a ten-lane highway packed with traffic.
In a single frame, it captured a contradiction that has become so normalised. We see the blue sky and conclude the air is clean. We see the “good” rating and assume the danger has passed.

While seasonal forest fires trigger nationwide concern and frustration, our most persistent source of harmful air pollution is not drifting in from afar. It is idling outside school gates, flowing along suburban roads, and passing us every day on highways just like the one in that photograph.

Vehicle emissions account for up to 70% of urban air pollution. Yet because we cannot easily see them, we rarely treat them with the same urgency. One of the most significant threats to public health remains hidden in plain sight.
Pollution we fear, pollution we accept

When haze hits, we pull children indoors, stock up on N95 masks, and worry about long-term health damage. Yet year-round, invisible tailpipe pollution exposes us to microscopic particulates, nitrogen dioxide, and ground-level ozone.
These pollutants penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream. They are linked to asthma, impaired lung development, cardiovascular disease, stroke and dementia.
Because these harms accumulate slowly rather than announcing themselves with burning eyes or irritated throats, we often treat them as an unavoidable part of modern life.
Children at the front line
Consider the daily routine outside almost every school. Children weave through rows of idling cars and motorcycles while parents wait with engines running and air conditioning switched on.

We would think twice about making a child stand beside an exhaust pipe. We panic when toxic haze blankets the country. Yet we have normalised school pickup arrangements that expose children to traffic pollution every single day.
The contradiction extends inside our vehicles.

Many people imagine the car interior as a protected space, but in heavy traffic ventilation systems draw in exhaust from surrounding vehicles. Pollutant concentrations inside cars can often exceed the ambient levels reported by regional monitoring stations.
We seal ourselves inside glass-and-steel boxes, convinced we are sheltered from the very pollution we are helping to create.
Unequal exposure
The burden is not distributed equally.

Millions of people live near major roads and expressways. Think of the apartments lining the Ampang-Kuala Lumpur Elevated Highway (Akleh) or landed homes built alongside the Lebuhraya Damansara–Puchong (LDP). Even with windows closed, fine particles can infiltrate indoor spaces.
For commuters waiting at bus stops along busy arterial roads, a “good” air quality reading can be almost meaningless. Exposure at street level often bears little resemblance to citywide averages.
Air pollution is not experienced as a statistic. It is experienced where people live, walk, wait, and breathe.
The other pollution
Traffic generates more than dirty air. It also produces noise.

Chronic exposure to traffic noise has been linked to hypertension, heart disease, stroke, hearing damage, stress, anxiety, sleep disruption, and impaired childhood development. Yet heavily modified cars and motorcycles continue to rumble, rev and backfire through our streets every day.
The health and peace of the wider public are routinely sacrificed so that a small minority can satisfy the need to draw attention to themselves.
Why EVs are not enough
Electric vehicles offer important benefits, but they do not solve the problem entirely.
EVs eliminate tailpipe emissions and reduce vehicle noise, yet they still generate pollution through tyre wear, brake dust and road-surface abrasion.
Because many EVs are heavier than their petrol-powered counterparts, some of these non-exhaust emissions can be substantial.

Replacing every petrol vehicle with an electric one would reduce exhaust fumes, but it would not eliminate the airborne rubber particles and roadway dust that already make up a significant share of urban particulate pollution.
The real solution
Cleaner fuels and electric vehicles are improvements, but they are ultimately technological band-aids.

Truly addressing urban air pollution requires reducing our dependence on private motor vehicles altogether. It means designing cities where walking, cycling and public transport are the default choices rather than desperate alternatives.

It means prioritising human lungs over vehicular throughput: building wide, shaded pedestrian corridors separated from traffic, reallocating road space to efficient bus networks, and creating dense, walkable neighbourhoods where daily necessities do not require a car trip.
Seeing beyond the blue sky
Clear skies can be deceiving.

Much of the harm caused by air pollution cannot be seen, but it is no less real because of that fact. We do not dismiss the germs that cause food poisoning simply because they are invisible. It is equally absurd to ignore the pollutants produced by our addiction to cars simply because they cannot be photographed.

The challenge ahead is not merely cleaner air. It is recognising that our car-dependent way of life carries hidden costs that are paid with our health, our peace, and our quality of life. Only when we acknowledge those costs can we begin the work of eliminating them.

ebf0d535f3f1459b: WASHINGTON: The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday said it had reached a staff-level agreement with Argentina on the third review of the country's bailout, potentially unlocking about US$900 million for the Latin American country.
The agreement is subject to approval by the IMF's executive board, after which the tranche can be disbursed to the Argentinian government.
In 2025, as it dealt with rampant inflation and currency depreciation, Argentina concluded an extended fund facility agreement with the IMF worth around US$20 billion over four years.
Since then, president Javier Milei has instituted a wide-ranging reform plan involving slashing public spending and reining in inflation.
The social spending cuts instituted by his government - with the IMF's approval - have been deeply unpopular, prompting frequent protests.
Since Milei took office in December 2023, inflation has dropped from triple digits to the current 33.5%.
In a statement on Tuesday, the IMF said Milei's reform programme had delivered "impressive results."
It lauded a marked improvement in the country's fiscal buffers and foreign exchange reserves.

It also praised the structural reforms instituted by the government "in the areas of trade, labor, investment and capital markets," saying they were "enabling a more efficient and market-based economy."
Part of the agreement for the release of the latest tranche of the bailout involved pledges from the Argentinian government to deliver further promises on both fiscal and monetary policy.
On the fiscal side, the IMF said Argentina had committed to delivering a primary surplus of 1.4% of GDP this year and next.
In terms of monetary policy, the central bank would take actions to support disinflation and reserve accumulation, while allowing exchange rate flexibility within a band, the IMF said.
On the reform agenda, the IMF said priority would be given to deepening domestic capital markets and expanding access to longer-term financing, among other steps.
Argentina is the IMF's largest debtor and has US$1.2 billion in debts to the Fund due this year, with a further US$7.8 billion due next year.
While Milei's government has succeeded in reining in runaway inflation, economic performance has been lacking in other key areas.
Consumer activity is anemic while debt defaults are skyrocketing.
Mortgage defaults have tripled over the past year, hitting 12.8%, the highest level in 20 years.
Growth remains sluggish and earlier this month the IMF downgraded its forecast for GDP expansion to 2.1% in 2026.

acd9154ed738c734: From Moaz Nair
According to an opposition lawmaker, the government providing subsidies is like “giving fish to the people”. Eventually, they say, the people will become lazy.

Critics frequently echo this sentiment, arguing that giving cash aid and relief to lower- and middle-income groups acts as a drag on national output. They view it as a pure consumption cost that fails to enhance economic productivity.
However, empirical macroeconomic data suggests this perspective is deeply flawed.
Far from being simple welfare relief, targeted cash transfers — such as Malaysia’s Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) — serve as vital mechanisms for strategic economic investment.
When structured effectively, cash assistance significantly amplifies both immediate aggregate demand and long-term labour productivity.

To make the full transition into a high-income nation, our fiscal discourse must evaluate how cash assistance behaves when scaled to the middle 40% (M40) income group. We need to shift the paradigm from merely maintaining a socio-economic floor to actively constructing an upward economic ladder.
The B40 multiplier effect
To understand the productivity debate, one must first isolate the short-term stimulus created by lower-income households, which is driven by a high marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
Because B40 families operate near subsistence levels, they immediately re-inject almost every additional ringgit received into the economy for basic necessities.
This capital flows directly into local micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) whose owners, in turn, pay suppliers and workers.
Studies reviewed by the World Bank demonstrate that cash transfers consistently yield a high economic multiplier, where every RM1 distributed generates upwards of RM2 to RM2.50 in local GDP growth.
Beyond immediate retail velocity, mitigating extreme financial stress unlocks long-term labour output by alleviating cognitive load and physical deprivation.
Cash aid provides the financial breathing room necessary for individuals to undergo technical and vocational education and training (TVET) or make the transition towards higher-value employment.
Furthermore, when paired with healthcare initiatives like PeKa B40 (ProtectHealth B40), cash transfers improve nutritional status and preventive care, fostering a healthier, more alert workforce.

This intervention yields its greatest dividends in future human capital, as targeted aid is reinvested into children’s education, mitigating school dropout rates and systematically elevating the skills ceiling of the next generation.
Not a policy panacea
Nevertheless, economists caution that cash handouts alone do not constitute a policy panacea.
While cash aid triggers rapid market circulation, it can induce minor, localised demand-pull inflation if supply chains face structural constraints.
It also carries a latent risk of welfare dependency if the programme lacks clear exit policies.
Financially, the model relies heavily on state revenue, requiring meticulous fiscal balancing despite indirectly bolstering tax revenues through increased economic activity.

Ultimately, cash aid only drives lasting productivity if it is structurally integrated with broader reforms, such as wage restructuring, digital transformation for small businesses, and proactive job placement programmes.
Upward social mobility for the M40
The economic dynamics shift fundamentally when evaluating the potential of expanding cash assistance or fiscal relief to the M40 income group.
Funding the M40 results in a lower immediate economic multiplier but yields a significantly higher long-term return on high-value productivity.
While B40 interventions focus primarily on survival, aid targeted at the M40 drives upward social mobility and formal structural investment.

Because their baseline survival needs are secured, M40 households exhibit a lower MPC and direct surplus funds towards professional education upgrades, debt reduction, healthcare insurance, and domestic tourism.
While this slower velocity of money tempers the immediate multiplier effect, it channels institutional capital into formal consumer sectors that employ a vast segment of the domestic workforce.
As the backbone of the nation’s skilled workforce, reducing cost-of-living pressures on the M40 unlocks high-value labour productivity through two primary channels:

Professional upskilling: M40 individuals are highly likely to utilise financial relief or tax-rebate equivalents to fund professional certifications or postgraduate diplomas. This creates a talent pool capable of anchoring high-value foreign direct investment (FDI).

Mitigating burnout: It eases the intense economic pressures faced by the “squeezed middle” — a demographic often ineligible for heavy subsidies yet highly vulnerable to inflation — thereby stabilising white-collar productivity.
Furthermore, unlike the B40, a portion of the disposable income left with the M40 enters the broader financial ecosystem as productive capital.
These individuals channel surplus funds into unit trusts, voluntary Employees Provident Fund (EPF) contributions, or retail equities, deepening national investment liquidity.
This liquidity also enables M40 professionals to seed side hustles, micro-digital enterprises, and freelance consulting ventures, fostering broader innovation across the digital economy.
Conclusion
Ultimately, the core differences between funding these two socio-economic tiers lie in their macroeconomic outcomes.

While the B40 target impact drives immediate retail consumption, rapid market velocity, and basic labour survival through direct cash transfers, the M40 target impact enables discretionary spending, high-value professional upskilling, and managerial efficiency through delivery mechanisms like tax reliefs, education credits, and housing incentives.
Maximising Malaysia’s economic potential requires a balanced, dual-track approach rather than an adversarial policy debate.
Funding the B40 establishes the vital economic and social floor, ensuring the baseline labour force remains stable, healthy, and participant in the economy.

Conversely, providing targeted relief to the M40 builds the economic ladder, offering the upward momentum necessary to push the workforce out of the middle-income trap and into high-productivity industries.
True economic foresight lies in managing both ends of this continuum simultaneously.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

0f39ea2acf21946d: The Malaysian legal system, largely inherited from the British adversarial model, offers a legal framework that stands in stark contrast to the inquisitorial approach favoured by major religions.
The difference lies in philosophy. Inquisitorial traditions are designed to seek fairness, truth, and community responsibility, while adversarial systems tend to prioritise procedure and advocacy.
This is one of the chief causes of the massive case backlogs plaguing our courts.

Malaysia is not alone. Across the Commonwealth, chief justices and judiciaries have yet to recognise the wisdom of moving away from adversarial and aristocratic procedures inherited from their former colonial masters. These outdated practices remain the primary culprits behind endless delays.

By contrast, the Panchayat system in India—a council of village elders employing inquisitorial methods—delivers fair and immediate justice. I have personally witnessed this in my ancestral village of Thopputhurai, Vedaranyam, Tamil Nadu.
That experience later became the foundation for my University‑cum‑Court Annexed Arbitration (UCCA) model, designed to clear case backlogs.

Litigants and the public want immediate solutions to their disputes and hope for instant decisions. Instead, they are subjected to the opposite: a long, convoluted process culminating in lengthy, wordy judgments issued by the trial and appellate courts.

From my observation as both lawyer and judge, the adversarial system has little to do with genuine justice or fairness. Instead, it rewards those who can present their version of the truth most convincingly.
Quite often, being “economical” with the truth can secure a win. In most cases, it becomes a contest of who can craft the more compelling narrative.
In such a scenario, an advocate’s role is to construct a persuasive narrative based on selective facts to sway the judge. Whether the narrative reflects truth or reality is secondary.

More often than not, trial judges are not subject‑matter experts and simply act as arbiters of competing narratives. On the other hand, when a trial judge is an expert in the field, truth and falsehood in both evidence and submissions can be quickly discerned.
The tragedy is that our system rarely prioritises such expertise. Instead, the Commonwealth suffers from backlogs generated by courtroom rhetoric—often pursued for financial gain.

The British aristocratic litigation procedure imposes no strict timeframe on the legal fraternity or judiciary, leaving justice perpetually delayed. Consequently, the legal maxim “justice delayed is justice denied” has become the defining failure of Commonwealth courts, a shameful hallmark of their dysfunction.

The UCCA model offers a way forward. By appointing subject‑matter experts of unquestionable integrity—chosen by disputing parties after a conflict arises—false rhetoric can be dismantled and backlogs eliminated. Such a system would restore credibility to the process and return justice to being timely, fair and accessible.

Through the mercy of the Almighty, the UCCA path may witness the return of the legal profession’s soul, reminding lawyers and judges alike that their calling is not to perpetuate delay or profit from complexity, but to uphold justice as a sacred trust.
In this way, the profession can recover its moral compass, aligning itself once more with the values of major religions that emphasise truth, compassion and accountability.

I trust that my three previously published articles"Is the British litigation system a failure?", "Justice not a privilege, costs not a weapon" and "Academia can rescue democracy’s spoilt child" —will together offer a definitive pathway to addressing the challenges faced across the Commonwealth, helping to restore public faith in the judiciary while saving governments billions of dollars.

Timely justice is not merely a procedural expectation, it is an unwritten constitutional right. The legal industry and the judiciary are strictly obliged to uphold it. When they fail, they risk being seen by the lay public as scammers, not guardians of justice.

I have studied this crisis for over two decades. My firm conclusion is that the legal industry and judiciary have failed in their constitutional duty to deliver timely justice, eroding public trust and undermining the very legitimacy of the courts.

Chief Justices across the Commonwealth would serve the public well by coming together to confront the backlog crisis and work toward resolution. Such gatherings must go beyond rhetoric and commit to structural reform.
The UCCA model offers them the opportunity to revamp their court systems. It can help dismantle the culture of delay, restore faith in the judiciary, and reaffirm the profession’s higher calling.

5c819a565532267f: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely — or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions.

In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread.

South Carolina's measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania's ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it.

7abd964f26d9f004: Venezuela could become an early adopter of China’s AI-powered mass surveillance systems.
Originally published on Global Voices
Former president of Venezuela Nicolás Maduro with current Interim President Delcy Rodríguez and Chinese ambassador in Venezuela Lan Hu. Photo by Probox. Used with permission.

This article was originally published by ProBox on September 21, 2026. An edited version is republished by Global Voices thanks to a media partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Venezuela may be one step away from becoming one of the first countries outside the People’s Republic of China to adopt the new generation of Chinese artificial intelligence systems for mass surveillance and political control, according to a report from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI).

The report reveals that in July 2025, the Venezuelan government signed a memorandum of understanding with iFlytek, a Chinese company that has been on the U.S. trade sanctions list since 2019 for its role in the repression of Muslim minorities in Xinjiang. The agreement to jointly develop Artificial intelligence in Venezuela was negotiated by Delcy Rodríguez, then vice president and now Venezuela’s interim president.

The report was written by Fergus Ryan, Bethany Allen, and Nathan Attrill of ASPI’s Cybersecurity, Technology, and Security Program, along with external contributors Mariví Marín (executive director of ProBox), Shannon van Sant, and analyst Alex Colville. The report was published in September 2026 by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, with funding from the Human Rights Foundation.
An infrastructure that was already in place

The report, titled “Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of Chinese AI-Enabled Digital Authoritarianism”, documents that Venezuela doesn’t need to build a surveillance system from scratch — it already has one, built largely on Chinese technology through importing cameras, networks, identity systems and command centres from Chinese firms in the past two decades.

While the resulting architecture is fragmented, unevenly deployed and technically constrained, ASPI's researchers identified six interconnected technological layers in the imported surveillance system: telecommunications, digital identity, central databases, video surveillance, internet control, and now, analytics and artificial intelligence. All of them were built or enhanced with support from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, CEIEC, Hikvision, and Dahua.
Graphic made by Probox. Used with permission.

At the core of this system’s identity layer is the Carnet de la Patria (Homeland Card), a digital ID linked to social benefits. The report states it had 21.8 million registered users as of January 2023—roughly three-quarters of Venezuela’s population—and served as many as 14.2 million people each month. A layer of central databases could cross-reference identity information, biometric data, and social welfare data.

The report also describes a network of video surveillance and command centres (such as the VEN911 and SIMA systems) capable of monitoring public spaces and coordinating responses in real time, and a telecommunications infrastructure that, by channelling a large portion of the country’s data traffic, functions as an additional checkpoint.

While the above technologies were imported through separate contracts, they reinforce one another and form a partially connected surveillance system, enabling government agencies to identify, monitor, and take action regarding citizens’ behaviour.
What changes with the integration of AI?

According to the report, iFlytek's AI technology will further integrate the pre-existing layers of surveillance infrastructure into a more comprehensive system, making it faster, more scalable, and harder to evade.

Facial recognition, voice identification, and automated database cross-referencing tools could be used to identify, locate, and profile individuals without any visible human action, such as attending a protest.

iFlytek is one of the world’s leading providers of voice recognition and content moderation technology. The same report explains that the company promotes a product capable of detecting “more than 100 types” of politically sensitive content in voice messages, and that its technology is integrated into China’s judicial and censorship system.

iFlytek itself already sells a voiceprint identification service that compares recordings against a database to identify a person among thousands; this is precisely the same technology the company has provided to public security authorities in Xinjiang, according to ASPI's report.

If that capability were combined with the network of cameras and the identity records in the Carnet de la Patria, the risk is that the government would no longer need to rely on someone’s visible participation in a protest to identify them, and could instead preemptively flag individuals based on patterns of association, movement, or activity on social media even before any specific incident occurs.

Added to all this is a pattern of opacity. As has been the case for years with technology agreements between Venezuela and the People’s Republic of China, the details of the memorandum with iFlytek have not been made public in their entirety; this makes it difficult to ascertain the actual scope of the agreement, which is why the report recommends demanding the full publication of these agreements.

Despite this lack of transparency, there is at least one precedent that the government itself has publicly acknowledged. In January 2025, the National Chamber of Popular Self-Government was launched—a command center that centralizes information from thousands of community councils and districts across the country—which Maduro described as operating “with Chinese technology and artificial intelligence.”

The agreement with iFlytek was signed months before Maduro’s capture by U.S. forces in January 2026. Delcy Rodríguez, who negotiated it directly at the time, now serves as the U.S.-backed interim president. However, the report notes that during her tenure, the Venezuelan surveillance apparatus has not been dismantled. This is the same conclusion reached by the UN International Fact-Finding Mission, which documented that the surveillance infrastructure remained in place following the change in government.

The authors argue that, despite this, there is a window of opportunity. The interim government’s current dependence on the U.S. could be used to demand the cancellation of the memorandum with iFlytek before this technological escalation is implemented.
What can be done?
Given the risks that China’s technological cooperation poses to human rights in Venezuela, the report offers seven recommendations:

Support Venezuelan civil society by increasing funding, protection, and training in digital security for organizations and journalists under threat, and by expediting humanitarian visas for those who are being persecuted.
Provide free access to AI tools so that civil society can circumvent censorship and protect itself from government surveillance.
The U.S. should demand that Rodríguez immediately cancel the memorandum with iFlytek, before it is fully integrated into the surveillance systems.
Have the Secretary of State press Rodríguez to dismantle the current surveillance system, including the “Carnet de la Patria”.
Plan for liberal reform by drafting privacy laws and oversight mechanisms now, in preparation for when political openness emerges.
Impose sanctions for abuse of surveillance by expanding penalties to include officials and companies that facilitate digital repression.
Establish security standards for foreign AI used by governments, including independent evaluation and transparency about the origin of the models.
Written by ProBox

67f0b179673ce3b4: Like many leaders today, Prabha Jha has been feeling the significant impact artificial intelligence is having on business operations. While the rapid evolution of the technology can bring fear, uncertainty, and confusion, Jha chose a different response: excitement. She began asking herself, “How do I become part of this once-in-a-lifetime thing?”  Jha holds a bachelor’s degree in information technology from the University of Calcutta and earned her MBA while working at Verizon, where she continues to build her career. As she looked for an educational opportunity to engage more deeply with AI, MIT quickly emerged as a natural choice.  Growing up, Jha viewed MIT as “the mecca for anybody who is in engineering and technology,” so she naturally turned to the Institute when seeking an opportunity to learn about AI. Unlike other programs that took place fully online, MIT xPRO’s AI for Senior Executives stood out to Jha primarily because it offered an in-person component that allowed her to meet and connect with peers.  Jha decided to take the leap. She acknowledges that the program was a significant investment of both time and money, but ultimately views it as one of “the best decisions [she] made” — one she “would do all over again if [she] had to.” The experience gave Jha the opportunity she was looking for to invest in herself and strengthen her skills in AI. It also provided her with invaluable professional relationships and the confidence to develop multiple AI solutions for Verizon. Putting those news skills and relationships to work, she co-wrote, with some of her peers, “The AI Anthology,” a collection of AI insights designed to support other leaders navigating similar challenges with AI.  An unexpected learning obstacle Jha’s learning journey wasn’t without its curveballs, though. Just two months before she was set to complete the program, she spent two weeks in the hospital with a severe infection and was unable to graduate with her original cohort. With the help of MIT staff, she joined the next cohort, giving her an unexpected opportunity to spend another five days on campus with 100 brand-new peers.  “You just never know what curveball life can throw and what it might be there for,” Jha says. What initially felt like a setback turned into an unexpected benefit. Jha valued the opportunity to meet new people and spend more time on campus. She also appreciated that just six months later, the program’s content had already been refreshed. Those additional “five days of immersion” became a vital part of Jha’s learning journey, giving her and her peers more time to collaborate face-to-face and learn from one another.  “I think it was eye-opening to be able to meet so many people with diverse backgrounds and geography, and then we connected at the human level,” she says.  Jha particularly valued that sense of connection in the context of learning about AI, a field that, she acknowledges, comes with fears, vulnerabilities, and difficult questions. Learning alongside peers with different professional and cultural backgrounds gave her new perspectives and added another dimension to the experience. Jha estimates that “30 percent of what I was learning was from the program, material, and professor [while] 70 percent was my peers and the interactions.” Peer discussions spark an idea The idea that would change the trajectory of Jha’s time in the program came during a “salon gathering” at the home of Manolis Kellis, a professor in MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. As students shared personal stories about their experiences with AI, one story in particular stayed with Jha: that of one of her peers, whose motivation to explore AI solutions stemmed from her work to find a cure for her mother’s Alzheimer's disease and dementia.  At that moment, Jha realized that AI is personal. She still “gets goosebumps thinking of that moment where AI really became human and a connecting point.” She saw the value in capturing these diverse perspectives and experiences with AI that go beyond operational efficiency and revenue growth, and wanted to continue the conversation beyond the program. Jha expressed to her peers an interest in capturing these stories and connections in a book. One year later, Jha and 20 other leaders released “The AI Anthology,” a collection of essays examining the influence AI has had across industries and across society.  One of the biggest takeaways from the AI for Senior Executives program — and one that Jha hopes readers will take from her book — is the importance of thinking differently.  Jha believes leaders may be missing a fundamental shift: “We are still kind of stuck in this traditional measurement of success,” she says. “We cherish revenue; we like cost-cutting and time-saving, and converting them to dollars.”  While Jha acknowledges this mindset makes sense in corporate America, she believes leaders must move beyond it in order to find more empowerment through AI and its capabilities. She notes that future generations are already asking different questions, including: “What can I get in the quality of my life?” and “How can I use my time in a way that is fulfilling for me early on?”  The future of embracing AI for business and a better world  Jha recognizes that AI adoption is not optional for businesses, and that everyone must learn about and embrace it. At the same time, she is a steadfast believer in AI’s ability to create a better world. Instead of viewing AI as a foregone burden, she sees it as a “transformation unlike any other” that is providing us with the opportunity to overcome insecurity, adapt and grow, and invest in ourselves.  In her work at Verizon, Jha takes seriously the company’s role as “a brand name for reliable, quality service” providing “critical infrastructure” to groups, such as first responders or children, who depend on their services. This responsibility comes with a privileged obligation to participate in and protect society, and Jha finds it empowering that AI can help enable this. In her own experience, she’s appreciated the ability to accelerate progress and impact, when she may have previously needed to rely on a larger team.  So, what’s next for Jha? Currently, she is working on a new initiative focused on supporting small and medium-sized businesses that are navigating AI implementation. Her goal is to help them understand what tools they need, how AI fits into their specific operational model, and how they can measure success, so they can focus on their strengths as a business and how they can drive value.
