003a6a0d932a932b: I think a lot about time. How we consume it, save it, enjoy it, spend it. How it can be interminably slow or rush by before you know it.

Our language subtly instructs us about our concept of time: We are urged to “savor the moment”; we want to “be present.” Even store clerks bid us to “have a good day”, as if you control whether this 24-hour period will be good or not. You can, of course, try your best to have a good day, and sometimes succeed – unless the universe has other plans for you.1
I’ve always been fascinated by time; maybe that’s why I was so intrigued by watches as a kid. A few recent events have me thinking about time more than usual: a big birthday, a loss, other events …
Age

I never had a midlife crisis. Perhaps it was too cliché. Big round birthdays and aging never bothered me. The only experience I had relative to age was waking up on the morning of my 60th birthday and immediately thinking, “Start of the fourth quarter, down by 7 – you’re still in this thing, but lots to do. Get busy!”

The result was a new book, some personal projects, financial and estate planning, and less procrastination on major purchases, travel, and activities I had been putting off for no good reason. As an immortal, I would get around to them eventually. Once the 19-year-old in me admitted immortality was no longer operative, I suddenly felt an urgency to check off some boxes. No, not a bucket list, just a short inventory of unfulfilled desires I suddenly felt the urge to make happen.
Hey, wait a second…
Impermanence
Our house developed an exterior leak that dripped into the basement. To prep for the contractors, we cleared out a lot of accumulated junk. The big surprise: 6 MacBooks dating back to the 2000s.

Six! Each one was a thing: expensive, useful, important, yet oh so temporary. We were warned: “Don’t throw away old laptops unless you removed the hard drives!” Looking at these old, battered MacBooks, I remember the excitement of buying them: Faster, better, improved! When we buy something new, we forget it will eventually wear out, get damaged, become less useful, get replaced or discarded. Everything!
The second law of thermodynamics is a bitch.
Illusion

Here’s something you might not have considered: Time, at least as an objective concept outside human consciousness, doesn’t exist. It’s (mostly) a human creation; no chrono particles, no celestial timekeeper, no physical mechanism governs time’s passage. Our experience is an illusion, a function of our sensory inputs colliding with our consciousness…

Physics recognizes Time is a useful construct, a handy artifice for comparing forces relative to one another. “T” in equations is time as a dimension between other vectors. You use it to measure speed or distance, but mostly relative to each other. Every measure of time seems to quantify only an object’s motion, whether it’s the vibration of a Cesium atom or the hands on a clock.2

I wonder: Does Time exist independently of us, conscious beings? Without us, does the relative motion of objects in 3-dimensional space include time – or is that simply a convenient human assumption? 3

The flow of time seems especially illusory: The sense of RIGHT HERE AND NOW, the intersection of THIS instant (T) and THIS location (X, Y, & Z), is moving forward, a present “now” that advances tick by tick, second by second, and millennia by millennia. I struggle to believe this is anything other than the human mind trying to make sense of the experiential universe…
Our experience of Time, which changes so radically over our lives, is an illusion.
Money is Time
I contributed a chapter to the new book “How I Invest My Money Volume Two,” which was published this week.
Excellent financial advice needs specific personalization; I wanted to write something universal. My chapter, titled “Money Is Time,” is a tight 860 words, but has three concepts worth sharing:
First, Money is society’s measure of the economic contributions you make with your time (including effort, expertise, insight, skill, etc., which are themselves functions of time).

Second, we all get precisely 24 hours a day. Each of us is born wealthy in time, with endless, infinite hours, days, weeks, months, and years, which we fritter away when young. Later in life, we learn that time is our stock in trade.

And third, Money IS Time. Every purchase you make is an investment of your insultingly limited time. The days may be long, but the decades are short. Keep this front of mind as you spend your finite supply of time.
Time Travel
As a sci-fi fan, I’ve sat through more than my fair share of time-travel flicks. Screenwriters and novelists seem to ignore two issues.

The first is Location: When you travel back in time, the planet you’re standing on will have moved – millions or billions of miles away. The Earth orbits the Sun at 66,600 mph; the Sun makes a 260-million-year route around the Milky Way at 515,000 mph; even the Earth’s rotation is 1,040 mph. You must surmise your position relative to the galactic expansion at 515,000 mph, despite its occasional changes in acceleration. 4

In total, we are moving at 828,000 mph. Time travel for a century, and you space travel 725 billion miles (best of luck calculating that precisely). Off by a trillionth of a %, e.g., ~three-quarters of a mile, you materialize inside Earth’s crust (deadly) or nearly 4,000 feet in the air before gravity ends you. Greater errors deliver you into the vacuum of space.

My second issue is the Arrow of Time. It annoys me to send people into a nondeterministic future that hasn’t happened yet. I don’t buy the thesis of a Universe as a block of past, present, and future all occurring at once – it lacks causality.5

In my version of time travel, you can go into the past, but only to return to the point from which you departed. But you cannot visit the Restaurant at the End of the Universe because it hasn’t happened yet. Between now and then, many things will shape what actually happens. But until then, the future doesn’t exist.6
Dog Time

People often think of their lives in terms of blocks of time: You lived in this house or apartment; you worked at this job or that one; you dated or married this person. These blocks make up the eras of your life.

I sometimes think of my life in terms of dogs: Erev was a Labrador retriever I had as a kid; Killer was the stray I adopted in college (and my dad fell in love with); when we moved out of the city, we rescued Max, a shepherd-bearded mutt puppy; Jackson was a Labradoodle who kept Max young until he was 17. Lexi (died young of encephalitis), then Kodie (who is 5), followed Jack. Teddy, a Portuguese Water Dog, followed Max. We had to say goodbye to him last week, and even though I knew it was coming, the grief still shocked me.

Dogs gauge time by how your scent slowly fades since you left the house. If you return at the ~same time every day, they approximate that by how your scent declines over the day. They know when you are returning by that marker.

We all lose friends and family; our relationships are complicated, filled with joy, angst, baggage, walls, and emotions. None of that complexity exists with dogs – they are pure, unconditional love; when they depart, the wound finds you naked and defenseless…
Optionality

As you get older, you begin to realize you kinda know how the movie ends: what you’ve accomplished, what you’ve earned, the people you affected, and who affected you. Not a full accounting, but a modest recognition of who you have become.

It begins to set: You realize what is increasingly unlikely to occur. Projects that might take 5, 10, or 20 years to reach fruition, learning a new language, starting a business, learning to read music, seem difficult to impossible.
That is the biggest disillusionment about aging: What you gain in agency, you lose in optionality.

I’m not sure how persuasive that is to me. Also, attempts to quantize gravity, such as the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, has no T. Time vanishes from the equations entirely

It’s an adequate Nobel Prize-winning theory, at least until a better one comes along.

0efd9cf003b3b02d: Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult
Originally published on Global Voices

Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times. Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country (Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.
Altar to María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

These sites are part of the Cerro María Lionza Natural Monument, popularly known as the Montaña de Sorte, and they represent the most prominent expressions of this cult nationwide, so they are visited year-round by practitioners or “caravans” (as these groups are commonly called),
But few days are as important as October 11 and 12, when thousands of people flock there to celebrate the Day of Indigenous Resistance in Venezuela.

These dates offer an opportunity for ethnographic and cultural observation, specifically how oral histories and our ethnic origins are reclaimed; including those of Indigenous peoples, some of them warriors who fought against Spanish colonization, and African populations — enslaved people and maroons — as we can understand through the figure of the Three Powers: Queen María Lionza as the central figure of the cult, the leader, accompanied by El Indio Guaicaipuro and El Negro Felipe.
Altar to Queen María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

For this celebration families gather among the trees and along the banks of the Yaracuy River, which runs through the entire mountain, setting up lavish altars to the various deities of Venezuelan spiritualism, which embody the sacred rituals characteristic of the Marialioncero cult.

The figure of María Lionza is profound, and I believe it is risky to oversimplify her, as she is regarded as a Queen, a Goddess, a mother, and a guardian, yet there are also aspects linked to her sensuality, as evidenced by the iconographic representations of her that have emerged -naked or clothed, for example-.

In this regard, I draw upon the writings of Francisco Ferrándiz and César Escalona from the perspective of Venezuelan anthropology, combining them with my own observations and field interviews, to address issues related to gender and sexual diversity that are essential to the fascinating debate within the cult on its various courts — such as the Black Court, the Viking Court, the Malandra Court, the Chamarrera Court, and the Medical Court, among others — and entities.
Detail of flowers and bottles of the Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Gender diversity, gender discrimination

The Sorte Mountain is a setting where gender stereotypes are called into question, and I believe they undermine androcentric perspectives and rigid notions of masculinity and femininity found within Christianity, since the entities pose a challenge due to their wide spectrum in terms of strength, height, voice, attire, and other details of the mediums who embody them, as well as the particular characteristics of each spirit.
Strenght between banks and Viking Court entity. Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In his ethnographies and writings, Ferrandíz offers interesting reflections on the body and masculinity in this religion, and how male mediums (from a position of stigmatized masculinity) resisted possession by female spirits, something that did not occur as frequently among female spiritualists.
That is why my encounter in Sorte with the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers — led by Osmer Padrón and his godchildren — allowed me to also explore these aspects.
Osmer Padrón embodies the spirit of María Dolores. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

Osmer Padrón, Wander Rodríguez, and Jhonaiker Díaz are all male mediums that belong to the LGBTQ+ community, and are part of this caravan that channels female entities from the Black Court, such as María Dolores Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez, Rita Encarnación, and La Negra Tomasa; but in Osmer’s case, he also channels Mister Piter, a male entity from the Viking Court, a warrior and healer.

Wander tells me that in the LGBTQ+ spiritualist community, “there’s a lot of discrimination, both inside and outside the mountain [of Sorte], but Queen María Lionza is love and affection, and as many spiritual beings have said, we are all deeply cherished by her. We are here first and foremost to fulfill a mandate from Goddess and our Majesty María Lionza. Nothing else matters.”

Portraits of Jhonaiker Díaz (who works with the spirit of La Negra Tomasa) and José Rojas. They are part of the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Regarding the practice of channeling female entities from the Black Court, Rodríguez tells me:

Most of us spiritualists in the LGBTQ+ community dress up in dresses — or find ourselves transported into that state — not because we want to… Right now, there’s a lot of talk from people saying that men who want to be women channel Black Court entities just to wear dresses, but that’s not the case. When a spiritual entity is a woman or was a woman, she always seeks to be fully covered, to cover her breasts, and why? Because she feels exposed; she feels alive. There are many spiritual entities, such as the Negra I work with — who is Rita Encarnación Martínez Chávez — as well as María Dolores Rodríguez Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez Martínez, and Negra Tomasa, who have their dresses made for them. It’s not because we want to wear dresses; if they were our own bodies, we’d walk around shirtless, but no, they always… Spirituality always seeks to feel alive; that’s why they put on their dress, their turban, and some even seek out a flower.

Dresses for female entities from the Black Court: Francisca Martínez, Francisca Palacios, María Dolores Rodríguez, Negra Tomasa and Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

There are curious details regarding what the entities ask of their “banks” —people who also care for the physical forms of the entities — such as tobacco and aguardiente; but in the case of the black women, just as they ask for their dresses, they also ask for makeup and make gestures as if looking at themselves in a mirror.

Wander tells me that, in the case of Rita Encarnación, “her favorite flower is the cayena, since it was the flower with which she learned to perform her magic, while she labels “other flowers as hypocrites, since those other flowers remain alive for many days after being plucked from nature, whereas the cayena once plucked from nature wilt immediately.”
Altar to Las Tres Potencias (The Three Powers), in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

All of this demonstrates that Venezuelan spiritism must be examined through a gender lens, from a feminist perspective, reflecting on the power dynamics established between men and women, the presence of ritual cross-dressing during trance and possession rituals, and other aspects that enrich our understanding of this important Venezuelan religion.
Wander Rodríguez enters a trance to receive the spirit of Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Written by Freisy González
7c2863bae5f69e0c: From Hartini Zainudin
Last Thursday, a newborn boy was found alive in a box under the stairs of a Kepong apartment block. The next morning, a baby girl was found dead in a rubbish bin at a Bangsar waste site.
Police are investigating the first case under Section 317 of the Penal Code for abandonment of a child, and the second under Section 318 for concealment of birth.
Two babies, found a day and a few kilometres apart. One will grow up as a foundling, the other never got that chance.
I have spent much of my working life between these two outcomes: recovering abandoned babies, sitting with mothers once they are traced, and raising children of my own through adoption.
These cases share a root, and we keep refusing to name it.
Infanticide begins long before the birth

The women, family and community development ministry recorded 72 baby dumping cases in 2025 and 18 in the first quarter of 2026. Selangor alone logged 43 last year. These are only the babies we know about. Concealed births and deaths that never reach the police sit outside every statistic.

Our law already accepts that infanticide differs from murder. Section 309A of the Penal Code applies when a mother causes the death of her newborn while her mind is disturbed by childbirth. Legislators wrote that provision because they understood something our public conversation still ignores: women in these cases are usually in crisis themselves.

In my experience, they are young — often teenagers — and have hidden the pregnancy for months, sometimes even from themselves. They have seen no doctor and give birth alone, in a bathroom or a hostel room, in pain and terror.

Some of them became pregnant through rape or incest by someone in the same house. Some are migrant workers who know a pregnancy can cost them a permit, a job and a roof in the same week. By the time the baby arrives, months of silence have done their work. Panic does the rest.
We respond by hunting for them. A police appeal goes out, the comment sections demand the harshest punishment, and every other frightened girl in Malaysia learns one lesson: better to hide.
The boy in Kepong survived the box. He now faces a slower danger.

The Federal Constitution was written with children like him in mind. Section 19B of Part III of the Second Schedule presumes that a newborn found abandoned was born here to a mother who is a permanent resident.

Section 1(e) of Part II makes anyone born in Malaysia who is not a citizen of any other country a citizen by operation of law. Together, they are meant to ensure that no abandoned child in Malaysia grows up stateless.

In 2024, the government proposed amendments that would have weakened both protections. Civil society, including many of us who worked with foundlings for decades, pushed back hard, and those changes were withdrawn before the bill passed. The safeguards stand.

Where they fail is in practice. Foundlings still leave hospitals with undetermined citizenships. Families who adopt them wait years for documents. Some children reach school age, then adulthood, unable to prove what the constitution already says they are.
What that does to a child

A foundling without citizenship pays foreigner rates at government hospitals. He may struggle to sit for public examinations, apply for a scholarship, open a bank account, marry legally or register the birth of his own children. Statelessness travels down generations.
He also carries the story. Adopted and fostered children eventually ask where they came from, and the answer begins with a box, a drain or a surau doorstep.

What we owe that child is a life in which that beginning does not decide everything that follows: a name, a nationality, a family and a fair start. Whether he gets them depends on paperwork handled by adults he will never meet.
The education we keep postponing
Almost every case I have handled traces back to the same gap.
A girl who does not understand her own body cannot recognise a pregnancy early. A girl who has never been told that what her uncle or stepfather does to her is abuse, does not know she can report it.
A boy who has never learned about consent does not see himself as responsible. A young woman who has never heard of confidential health services does not know which door to walk through.
Malaysian schools do teach reproductive health, but too often it is diluted, rushed or delivered only as a moral warning, by teachers who were never trained to teach it.
Young people end up learning about sex from friends and online, and learning about pregnancy too late.

International evidence, including Unesco's reviews of sexuality education programmes, shows that age-appropriate education does not make young people more sexually active. It helps them delay sex, protect themselves, and recognise and report abuse.
For a girl living with incest, knowing the words for what is happening to her can be the difference between a police report and a hidden pregnancy.
What must change
Comprehensive, age-appropriate sexuality and consent education in every school, taught by trained teachers, with parents brought in from the start.
Confidential crisis pregnancy care inside the public health system, so a girl can deliver safely in hospital and relinquish her baby lawfully without being treated as a suspect.
A welfare-first protocol: a mother who is traced sees a doctor and a social worker before a police investigating officer.
Automatic citizenship for every foundling at birth registration: apply Sections 19B and 1(e) as written. No child should need a lawyer or an NGO to claim what the constitution already guarantees.
Track the survivors: where foundlings are placed, whether they are adopted, and whether they ever receive a MyKad.
A name

This week, a welfare department officer will choose a name for the boy from Kepong. It will go on a form beside a blank space where his mother's name should be. Whether the line below it reads "warganegara" is up to us.
The baby girl from Bangsar will need a name too, for a grave.

Both were failed long before they were found: by classrooms that stayed silent, clinics their mothers did not know they could enter, and a system that protects foundlings on paper and abandons them in practice.
We know where the failures are. We have known for years.
Hartini Zainudin is co-founder of Yayasan Chow Kit, founder of Kasih Madhya, and co-founder of Voice of the Children.

1a30c83a19add1c9: From P Kamalanathan
Last week, during a visit to AIMST University, I met a Form 5 student. He was accompanying his sister to enroll in the university.
The Form 5 student was a straight As student.
When I asked about his ambition, he looked down and said: "Datuk, I am tired."
He is not alone.

The National Health and Morbidity Survey (NHMS) tells us a painful truth: 26.9% of our students aged 13 to 17 suffer from depressive disorders, while 13.1% have had suicidal thoughts, and 9.5% have attempted suicide.
Let me repeat: One in four is depressed. One in 10 has tried to end his/her life.
When I was deputy education minister, overseeing five million students, we worried about UPSR and SPM results.
Today, the Ipsos 2025 survey shows 37% of Malaysian parents worry about their children's mental health more than academic quality, and even more than bullying or social media.
Our children are not failing exams. We are failing to see they are hurting.

Last year, the education ministry recorded 7,681 bullying cases, up from 6,528 the year before. Pisa 2025 reported 27% of Malaysian students are bullied several times a month, higher than the OECD average of 20%.
A Monash study found 16% experience cyberbullying. Behind every statistic is a child who goes to the toilet and cries alone.
The recent tragic incidents in Petaling Jaya and Kedah shocked the nation. But let us be honest: tightening security and installing CCTV alone will not heal trauma, shame, isolation and fear.
What we need is a shift from report cards to "wellbeing cards".
Our new National Education Plan 2026-2035 speaks rightly of Karamah Insaniah, or human dignity. Dignity does not mean only respect for others. It means teaching a child to respect his own mind.
That is why I wish to propose three urgent actions:
1. Make mental health screening routine, not reactive.
We screen eyesight, we screen BMI. Why not mental health?

Studies by Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) have shown that more than 60% of students show mild symptoms of depression, anxiety or stress, but only 33% are in the normal range. If we catch such symptoms early, we can save a life.
Schools should have biannual wellbeing screenings, which are confidential and conducted by trained counsellors, not discipline teachers.
2. Fix the counsellor ratio and protect their time.
Today one counsellor serves 500 students. How can one person listen to 500 stories?

A counsellor, teacher and friend, who has served for over 20 years in a secondary school, told me recently: "Datuk, we are not short of caring teachers. We are short of time. One teacher cannot be discipline warden, SPM marker, and counsellor all at once."

She explained that in schools, Saringan Minda Sihat is already conducted twice a year. Students identified as critical need counselling sessions and follow-up screening to see whether there is improvement.
So when many students need follow-up, the current counsellor ratio is definitely not enough.

She added that counsellors are not only handling mental health but also have to manage 'murid cicir' (dropouts), Ziarah Cakna (home visits), leadership programmes, vape, smoking and drug issues, character development, career education, UPU, PKSK, career pathways, tracking SPM and STPM leavers, and parent conferences, etc.
She strongly believes that counsellors need more protected time and a better counsellor-student ratio. I agree. She also suggested separating counselling from discipline duties.
We must aim for a ratio of 1:250 in urban schools and 1:200 in high-risk schools.
The HEAL Line 15555 by the health ministry has received 267,873 calls. That shows children want to talk. But they want to talk to someone they see daily, not a voice on the phone.
3. Build peer support, not just punishment.

Selangor's PeerZ model and Monash's Thrive Together 2026 initiative show that when students are trained to support each other, help-seeking increases. The Anti-Bullying Tribunal and Anti-Bullying Act 2026 are important for justice, but peer support is important for healing.
In Sentul where I grew up, my mother taught me: "Education without empathy is just information."
We have become excellent at providing information. We must now become excellent at providing empathy.
I told that Form 5 boy who I met at AIMST: Being tired is not failure. Tired is a signal. Like fever signals infection, tiredness signals you need rest, talk, help.
This Deepavali, we will light lamps outside. Let us also light lamps inside our children's minds. Do not ask your child, "What marks did you get?" but instead, ask "How did you feel today?"
Because a nation that produces straight As students but loses them to depression has not succeeded. It has failed.
P Kamalanathan is a former deputy education minister and an adjunct professor of Unitar International University.

68b8fa9b95dac59e: From Wan Agyl Wan Hassan
Malaysia’s debate over minimum e-hailing fares is about more than the price of a ride.
This raises a fundamental question: how do we protect drivers’ livelihoods without making everyday mobility more expensive for the public?
E-hailing has changed how Malaysians travel. It offers convenience, flexible earning opportunities and an important transport option in areas where conventional public transport remains inadequate.
For some commuters, it also provides the crucial connection between home and the nearest rail station.
Yet behind that convenience is an economic imbalance that deserves attention.

Drivers bear much of the cost of providing the service. Fuel, maintenance, insurance, financing and vehicle depreciation come out of their pockets. They also absorb the cost of travelling to pick-up points, returning without passengers and waiting between bookings.
These are legitimate concerns. However, increasing the minimum passenger fare does not necessarily resolve them.
What passengers pay and what drivers actually earn are not the same thing.
Consider two drivers. One completes a RM12 journey but waits another 45 minutes for the next booking.
Another completes two RM8 journeys over a similar period with little waiting time.
Depending on distance and operating expenses, the second driver could earn more despite charging less per trip.

This illustrates why driver welfare cannot be measured by individual fares alone. What matters is how much a driver retains after expenses and how many productive hours they achieve throughout the working day.
Our research into Malaysia’s e-hailing economy highlights the financial pressures faced by drivers.
Based on our operating-cost model, running a Perodua Bezza for e-hailing services costs approximately RM0.40 per kilometre, including fuel, maintenance, insurance and vehicle depreciation.
While this is an indicative estimate rather than an industry-wide benchmark, our findings highlight an important reality: drivers continue to incur costs even when they are not carrying passengers.
Travelling to pick-up points, repositioning between bookings and waiting for the next journey all affect their actual take-home earnings.
This is why proposals for a minimum base fare, distance tariff and time-based compensation require careful examination.

A five-kilometre journey through Kuala Lumpur during evening congestion is very different from a similar journey on a free-flowing suburban road. The distance may be identical, but the time commitment and opportunity to secure subsequent bookings are not.
Conditions also differ outside major cities, where drivers may face longer waiting periods and fewer passengers.
A uniform national fare formula could therefore benefit some drivers while disadvantaging others.
Without reliable information on actual operating costs, trip demand and driver utilisation, setting a statutory rate risks creating new problems even as it attempts to solve existing ones.
There is also the passenger to consider.

For many Malaysians, e-hailing is not a luxury. It is a practical transport option, particularly where buses are infrequent, rail stations are difficult to reach or travelling without a private vehicle is inconvenient.
In Greater Kuala Lumpur, some commuters depend on e-hailing for short journeys to MRT and LRT stations.
If that connection becomes disproportionately expensive, the entire public transport journey becomes less attractive.
Some may return to driving or riding motorcycles. Others may simply travel less.
Neither outcome should be dismissed when Malaysia is investing heavily in improving public transport accessibility.
However, affordable feeder services should not come at the expense of drivers.
If the government wants to encourage first- and last-mile connectivity, targeted subsidies, integrated ticketing and demand-responsive transit should be considered.
Drivers should not be expected to absorb the cost of achieving national public transport objectives.
This brings us to the more important regulatory question: should Malaysia focus on setting minimum passenger fares or protecting minimum driver earnings?

The Gig Workers Act 2025 provides an opportunity to examine this distinction. Through the Gig Workers’ Consultative Council, Malaysia now has a statutory mechanism for considering minimum earnings rates and formulas appropriate to different categories of gig work.

Rather than immediately imposing a uniform passenger fare floor, policymakers should examine whether minimum driver remuneration, supported by reasonable expense recovery, would offer more direct protection.

Such an approach must also address unpaid working time such as dead mileage. Protecting earnings only while a passenger is onboard may still leave drivers exposed to long periods of uncompensated waiting.

Platform accountability is equally important. Malaysia already has commission ceilings for e-hailing services, but regulators must ensure that deductions are transparent, existing requirements are enforced and drivers understand how their earnings are calculated.
Reducing commission ceilings may appear attractive, but its effects on platform viability, incentives, competition and passenger prices must also be assessed.

The wider institutional framework deserves attention. Transport regulation, worker protection and competition oversight involve different authorities. Whether Malaysia strengthens existing institutions or establishes additional regulatory arrangements, responsibilities must be clear and enforcement effective.
Creating another regulatory body will not automatically improve driver earnings if the underlying economic problems remain unresolved.

Before introducing binding fare formulas, Malaysia needs a credible assessment of driver operating costs, actual take-home earnings, unpaid mileage, working hours, platform deductions and passenger affordability.
The findings should guide regulation, not the other way around.

Drivers deserve fair remuneration for their time, effort and investment. Passengers deserve affordable and reliable mobility. Platforms need sustainable commercial conditions, while regulators must protect the wider public interest.
These objectives need not conflict, but achieving them requires evidence rather than assumptions.

Malaysia should not confuse higher fares with better livelihoods. The true measure of successful e-hailing regulation is whether drivers earn a reasonable return, passengers can still afford to travel and the transport system continues to serve both.
That is the equilibrium worth pursuing.
Wan Agyl Wan Hassan is the founder and senior adviser to MY Mobility Vision, a transport think tank.
